#6206. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6205. American Grows Maintenance Footprint in Miami

A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

The airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

“Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”

American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

#6202. Alaska Atmos Rewards Business Card Bonus: 90K Points Welcome Offer

The $195 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card currently has a huge bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. For context, this is the business card of the Atmos Rewards portfolio, the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian. This is a potentially lucrative card that has just undergone a refresh, and you can read my Atmos Rewards Business Card review here.

In this post I’d like to go over the details of the Atmos Rewards Business Card bonus, for anyone who may be considering applying. There are lots of reasons to get this card, particularly the incredible bonus.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card with 90K bonus points

The Atmos Rewards Business Card currently has a welcome offer of 90,000 Atmos Rewards bonus points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, meaning the 90,000 points are worth $1,350 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Atmos Rewards points, for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, oneworld partners, and non-alliance partners.

Atmos Rewards points have all kinds of uses, ranging from booking short haul one-way economy awards on American for 4,500 points, to booking Starlux business class one-way awards from the US to Asia for 75,000 points. Of course capacity controls apply, so patience and flexibility will be required to get the best deal. Still, I find this to be one of the most useful points currencies out there.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card 90,000-point offer is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that we’ve seen on the card since it launched in August 2025 (which is when the Atmos Rewards program formally launched). How do the previous Atmos Rewards Business Card bonuses compare?

As you can see, the Atmos Rewards Business Card sign-up bonus has varied from 70,000 points to 90,000 points, and the current bonus of 90,000 points is the best publicly available offer we’ve seen. So if there has ever been a time to apply for this card, this is it.

When it comes to getting approved for the Atmos Rewards Business Card, what rules should you be aware of? There are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Bank of America policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

This one-time promotion is limited to company level Business Card clients opening a new account in response to this offer and will not apply to requests to convert existing accounts.

The good news is that eligibility for the Atmos Rewards Business Card is considered completely independently of any other cards in the portfolio, so you’re eligible if you have either of the personal Atmos Rewards credit cards. Many people even report being eligible for the Atmos Rewards Business Card (including the bonus) if they’ve had it in the past.

Beyond that, Bank of America doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for business cards. While Bank of America has the 2/3/4 rule and 3/12 rules, those apply to personal cards, and not business cards. Generally those with a Bank of America banking relationship also have the best odds of approval (though it’s by no means a requirement).

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to have to be approved for this card, though personally I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

Applying for this card won’t count as a further card toward Chase’s 5/24 rule, in case that’s a limit you’re trying to stay under.

Beyond the great bonus, there are multiple reasons to consider the $195 annual fee Atmos Rewards Business Card:

If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency, then having this card should be a no-brainer. The benefits really add up, between the lounge passes, the first checked bag free, preferred boarding, savings on inflight purchases, and more.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has introduced a best-ever welcome offer, whereby you can earn 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending.

This is an exceptional bonus, and this card is absolutely worth picking up for the points, especially given that eligibility isn’t mutually exclusive with other Atmos Rewards cards. In the long run, the card can be worth it for the perks for travel on Alaska and Hawaiian.

Anecdotally I find Bank of America business cards to be quite easy to get approved for, including if you’ve had the card in the past. Applying for this card also shouldn’t count as a further card toward the Chase 5/24 limit, if that’s of concern to you.

Anyone plan to pick up the Atmos Rewards Business Card with this great offer?

Taking a cruise is even better when you get a great deal — and if you’re looking to book right now for a cruise (or cruises) in 2027 and beyond, your timing couldn’t be better. Cruise lines have launched Black Friday deals that include discounted fares, cabin upgrades, third- and fourth-guest-free promos, and onboard credits.

We’ve found the best promotions from leading ocean and river cruise lines, lesser-known small-ship operators and expedition brands. So whether your goal is beach time in the Caribbean, wildlife-spotting in Alaska, seeing the northern lights in the Arctic or enjoying culture and cuisine along Europe’s rivers, there’s a deal for every type of cruiser.

When considering Black Friday offers, however, remember that cruise demand remains high, so selection may be limited and fares — especially on the newest ships — will likely be pricier than in years past. To truly get a good deal, make sure you’re comfortable with the final price quoted, including the exact fare per person and the value of any added perks, before booking. Calling the cruise line’s reservations department may help clarify any questions.

Here’s a look at the Black Friday deals being offered by more than 40 cruise lines. Check back soon for Cyber Monday deal updates.

Through Dec. 3, AmaWaterways has a Black Friday offer that lets you choose between a complimentary pre- or postcruise land package or cruise fare savings of up to $2,500 per cabin (double occupancy). You’ll also receive a free cabin upgrade on select 2027 and 2028 sailings in Europe and South America.

Small-ship operator American Cruise Lines’ current cruise deals and special offers include free domestic airfare and savings of $1,000 to $2,000 per cabin on select late 2026 and 2027 departures. This applies to its eight-night Florida Gulf Coast and Keys sailings, eight-night Southeast Sea Islands cruises, eight-night Columbia and Snake River sailings, and eight-night Lower Mississippi River cruises.

From Nov. 24 to 28, you can enjoy Black Friday savings of up to 55% on select expedition cruises from Atlas Ocean Voyages and also receive air credit savings of up to $2,000 per suite on qualifying voyages. Through Nov. 23, guests and travel advisers may also submit priority reservations for eligible expeditions on the Atlas Ocean Voyages website ahead of the five-day Black Friday promotional event. Reservations will begin confirming Nov. 24, subject to availability, with Atlas Yacht Club members receiving first priority to secure special Black Friday savings once the sale begins.

Through Dec. 12, Avalon Waterways is offering a Black Friday Sales Event featuring free gratuities and free airfare on select 2027 European river cruises. Avalon’s offer also includes savings of up to $2,000 per couple on a Panorama or Royal Suite upgrade on certain 2027 departures.

The Black Friday Flash Sale at Azamara, available now through Dec. 4, includes up to $6,000 off per cabin on select sailings in the Mediterranean, South America, Japan and Alaska, plus up to $750 in onboard credit per cabin. The deal is valid on all four Azamara ships for sailings from January 2027 to April 2028. You can book a sale voyage online or via a travel adviser.

Carnival's Black Friday deals span Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday with promotions that include discounted fares (four-night sailings start at under $200 per person), $49 per person deposits, room upgrades starting at $1, "Kids Sail Free" offers on select cruises (in third and fourth bunks), discounted beverage and Wi-Fi and shore excursion packages, and up to $50 in onboard credits. Sales and promotions are rolling out through Dec. 1.

Celebrity Cruises has a rolling Black Friday promotion offering savings of 75% on the second guest in the cabin on hundreds of applicable sailings in 2027 and 2028, including Caribbean and Mediterranean voyages on its newest ship, Celebrity Xcel. There are also limited-time offers that include up to $1,000 in additional savings per cabin plus $100 savings on select European sailings. This offer, for example, is valid through Nov. 24.

Through Dec. 2, Greek cruise line Celestyal has a “Big Sailaway” Black Friday promotion offering savings of up to 50%, plus third and fourth guests in a cabin sail free, on 58 Mediterranean and Greek islands voyages (from three nights to 14 nights) departing between March 2027 and February 2028. Celestyal operates two mid-size ships, Celestyal Journey and Celestyal Discovery.

Italy-based Costa Cruises is celebrating the start of the holiday season with a Black Friday sale offering fares as low as $399 per person (double occupancy) on select departures through June 2027, when reserved by Nov. 30. The included regions are the Caribbean (on Costa Fascinosa and Costa Favolosa), the Canary Islands (on Costa Smeralda) and the Mediterranean (on Costa Pacifica, Costa Toscana, Costa Smeralda, Costa Fascinosa and Costa Favolosa).

Through Dec. 7, small luxury cruise line Cruise Croatia is offering Black Friday savings of up to $500 per cabin on select seven-night spring and summer 2027 Adriatic sailings between Dubrovnik and Split, Croatia.

Book by Dec. 2 to take advantage of the Seasonal Savings deal offered by luxury cruise line Crystal. Full World Cruise and Full Grand Journeys are excluded.

Through Dec. 7, the Cunard Black Friday event can save you up to 40% on select sailings aboard Cunard's four ships — Queen Elizabeth, Queen Victoria, Queen Mary 2 and Queen Anne — with fares starting at $999 per person. Your specific cabin will be assigned at a later date, but a full, nonrefundable payment is due at the time of booking.

You can also combine the Black Friday offer with Holland America’s "Have it All" premium fare, which adds four high-value amenities: shore excursions, specialty dining, Wi-Fi and a beverage package.

Available through Dec. 2, Hurtigruten’s annual Black Friday sale offers savings of up to 50% on its 2027 Original Voyages, including the Coastal Express, which has cruised the Norwegian coast since 1893. Hurtigruten is also offering savings of up to 30% on its all-inclusive Signature Voyages in 2027, which include the North Cape Line and the Svalbard Line.

#6200. Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female. Airlines will sometimes have special celebrations with all-female crews, so here’s an interesting twist on that.

Today is (apparently) International Men’s Day. We often see airlines commemorate International Women’s Day, but there aren’t many airlines that celebrate the equivalent for men… well, except Finnair! The airline has today operated its annual flight with an all-male crew. This was the case for Finnair flight AY1331, from Helsinki (HEL) to London (LHR), using an Airbus A350-900.

The crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also all men. So, why is this important? Finnair highlights how only around 10% of cabin crew at the airline are male, but the company hopes to see that number grow in the future.

I think this is a fun concept, and it would be nice to see a closer to 50/50 gender ratio in both the cockpit and cabin, as it would show that everyone is given a fair chance at such a career.

I think it’s worth acknowledging that at many airlines, hiring of flight attendants is still primarily or exclusively based on gender. Now, the policies do vary significantly by airline, but perhaps an extreme example is India’s largest airline, IndiGo, which only hires female flight attendants. It’s literally written on the application, that it’s a job for “Female Indian nationals.”

It’s all so strange, because the airline has this super enthusiastic page about the importance of diversity in the workplace, and says “all employment decisions are made solely on the basis of merit and qualifications, without regard to a candidate’s gender…” You mean except the single largest portion of your workforce, which is cabin crew?

What’s interesting is that while those gender restrictions exist in the cabin, roughly 18% of the carrier’s pilots are female, which is way above the global average of 7%. That’s obviously a conscious effort, so I guess the idea is that women can become pilots but men can’t become flight attendants.

In fairness, I suspect part of the motivation here is that IndiGo flight attendants share hotel rooms on layovers, and that is a bit more complicated with mixed genders. Then again, it seems easy enough to just try to pair male flight attendants on trips, so it’s hardly a hurdle that can’t be overcome.

While we’re used to seeing airlines celebrate International Women’s Day, it’s rare to see an airline celebrating International Men’s Day. Finnair has operated an all-male flight today, intended to highlight how only 10% of flight attendants at the airline are male, and the airline wants to change that. While an unconventional initiative nowadays, I think this is still pretty cool.

What do you make of Finnair’s all-male flight?

#6199. Amex Auto-Enrolling Card Members In Paperless Billing (Sorry, Dad!)

Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)…

With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:

We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

After that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

Now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it says this:

Not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

It’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary says something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress…

As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

What do you make of Amex’s switch to paperless billing?

Like many commenters here, I greatly prefer paper statements and will jump through whatever hoops Amex sets up in order to keep receiving them. I am not 90 years old - I am a millennial. It also makes it significantly easier to review the statements for fraudulent charges, refunds or other credits that may have posted incorrectly, etc. Statements are too easy to miss in email with all of the other messages that come in. #6198. Why United & American Airlines Are Fighting Over The Future Of Chicago O’Hare

Janice Chen | Abdul N Quraishi - Abs | Shutterstock | Simple Flying

At Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), a bitter turf war between United Airlines and American Airlines has escalated from lobbying into courtroom battles, aggressive schedule expansions, and federal intervention. Clashes over gate redistributions, including United's late-2025 gains and American's subsequent push to reclaim ground, have turned the airport's concourses into a tense contest between two legacy rivals. At the same time, soaring flight schedules have collided with airfield construction, prompting federal caps to head off gridlock.

What makes this showdown more than a routine squabble over airport real estate is how O'Hare's departure-based gate formula, local traveler loyalty, and delayed terminal expansion reshape both carriers' economics. From maneuvering around Spirit Airlines' Concourse G gates to confronting Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) daily flight limits and broader credit-card loyalty stakes, the fight tests just how far two airlines will go to defend or expand their foothold in America's heartland.

Unlike New York-JFK or LaGuardia airport, where FAA slot rules directly govern takeoffs and landings, gate access at Chicago O'Hare is governed by agreements between airlines and the City of Chicago under its airport use and lease framework. Across O'Hare's four terminals and nearly 200 total gates, airlines lease preferential-use gates alongside common-use facilities that support flights across the airfield. As coverage from Airways Magazine and Travel Weekly explains, holding more preferential gates directly supports larger flight banks, smoother turnarounds, and greater scheduling flexibility at a busy connecting hub.

Under O'Hare's use-it-or-lose-it allocation mechanism, gate assignments are tied closely to departure share and prior-year flight activity and are not treated as permanent, untouchable real estate. Airlines submit schedules and usage data, allowing the city's Department of Aviation to review activity and redistribute gates annually when utilization shifts. That formula creates a clear mathematical link between flying more flights and expanding or defending concourse space.

Departure volume carries so much weight in periodic gate redetermination, so the rulebook naturally rewards aggressive scheduling and penalizes carriers that let gates sit idle or pull back capacity. Even small single-digit shifts in gate counts across concourses such as Terminal 3 or Concourse G can alter how tightly an airline packs its banks. In practice, that structure makes every year an overall score marker where schedule discipline and flight volume directly shape future gate real estate.

Supported by its downtown Chicago headquarters and a leading gate footprint around 95 to 99 gates across O'Hare, United Airlines has treated the hub fight as a line-in-the-sand defense of its Midwestern stronghold, as noted by Reuters. Following late-2025 gate reallocation gains and CEO Scott Kirby's pledge not to lose a single gate at United's expense, the carrier has leaned hard into schedule growth to protect its departure share. Coverage from The Points Guy and CBS Chicago highlights how United rolled out a major 2026 expansion, adding new routes and increasing frequencies across dozens of existing markets, to lock in operational scale.

That schedule offensive has been paired with an aggressive push to match or fend off rival moves on the ground, including United stepping in to acquire Spirit Airlines' preferential-use gates G12 and G14 for $30.2 million during Spirit's restructuring. As Travel Weekly and Half as Interesting note, snapping up those Concourse G gates gave United extra room to support added flying while keeping rivals from capturing every available opening. Even when federal caps later trimmed peak-hour schedules from initial plans, United's sheer departure base and hub connectivity kept it positioned as O'Hare's dominant carrier.

For United, defending O'Hare also means holding off challengers on high-value domestic and international connecting flows until long-term terminal capacity comes online. The hope is that through pairing route expansion with targeted gate acquisitions and vocal executive messaging, United can accept and manage near-term scheduling friction rather than cede ground in its home city.

These two carriers continue to jostle for market share.

Facing a gate redetermination that shifted space toward United ahead of the October 2025 handover, American Airlines took the fight to court in May 2025, accusing the city of mishandling the redistribution process under the airport's use-and-lease framework. As documented in federal and state court filings from Justia, American challenged the reallocation only to see its efforts to halt the transfer fall short in federal court and later in Cook County Chancery Court. Even with its Terminal 3 footprint squeezed, standing at 66 gates per Chicago Department of Aviation facility data as of April 1, 2026, following reallocation adjustments that varied across reporting snapshots, American pressed ahead with schedule additions rather than conceding relevance in Chicago.

To claw back concourse space outside the city's annual formula, American, like United, moved quickly in Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy proceedings to acquire two preferential-use gates, G8 and G10, on Concourse G for $30 million. Based on information from Culture Guru, it is clear how strategic that purchase was for American: gates G8 and G10 sit right next to an existing Admirals Club lounge, giving ground crews and connecting passengers closer proximity and easier operations. Adding those two gates helped offset part of American's redetermination loss while reinforcing its push to build up departures across domestic and regional markets.

For American CEO Robert Isom, holding firm at O'Hare is a deliberate statement that American will not be pushed aside or treated as a secondary afterthought in Chicago. As Chicago Magazine highlights, Isom has framed O'Hare as a vital hub for local and connecting travelers while rolling out added flights to defend share. That combination of courtroom pushback, opportunistic gate buying, and schedule investment shows American fighting to keep its Midwestern hub intact despite steep headwinds.

Aggressive schedule padding collided directly with airfield construction constraints in spring 2026, prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a scheduling limits order on April 20, 2026, capping daily operations at 2,708 flights between 6:00 AM and 11:59 PM Central Time, as per Forbes.

After published peak schedules pushed past 3,038 to 3,080 daily operations, well beyond what taxiway rehabilitation, ramp work, and staffing could reliably handle, the agency intervened under Section 41722 to curb congestion and later extended the order through October 30, 2027. Enforcing half-hour limits ranging from 30 to 84 operations pushed carriers to trim excess frequencies, delay seasonal route starts, or upgauge aircraft rather than fly schedules that could not clear the ground cleanly.

That federal ceiling exposes how tightly the gate fight is bound to O'Hare's buildout, where the ORDNext expansion has seen its price tag climb from an initial $8.5 billion estimate to $12 billion while major milestones stretch toward 2034 and 2035. Some pieces have moved ahead, including Terminal 5's 10-gate addition, Concourse L's three-gate expansion, and a $1.455 billion contract for the 19-gate Concourse D, but the wider Global Terminal is not slated to open until 2034, as reported by The Points Guy. With new gates arriving slowly and taxiway work narrowing surface margins, airlines cannot just build their way out of the issue in the near term.

Instead, every incremental concourse opening or construction adjustment carries heightened stakes because overall capacity is constrained by active building zones and long taxi times. Multi-year phased delivery means carriers need to put schedule ambition against real-world ramp and runway throughput. In a constrained environment, regulatory flight caps and phased construction make every available gate a scarce asset.

Both airlines are competing massively for passengers at Chicago O'Hare Airport.

Co-branded credit cards and frequent-flyer loyalty ecosystems that generate billions of dollars in high-margin partner revenue for major US carriers have a lot to do with this story. As Half as Interesting explains, airlines rely on card issuers and loyalty partnerships for lucrative non-ticket cash flows that help underpin overall profitability. In a major metropolitan market like Chicago, home to deep corporate travel accounts and high-spending cardholders, winning local flyer preference means capturing everyday card spend and repeat mileage redemptions, not just filling seats.

That loyalty dynamic helps explain why Chicago carries outsized strategic weight compared with markets where American previously lost ground. American ceded shares in New York and Los Angeles and began to lean more on hubs in Philadelphia and Phoenix, leaving Chicago as a critical battleground if it wants to stay top-of-wallet among big-spending coastal and Midwestern flyers. Conversely, Travel Weekly highlights how hub scale and schedule breadth reinforce card acquisition, because travelers who cannot conveniently fly or connect on an airline tend to shift both their trips and their credit card spend elsewhere.

At the same time, executive debates over loyalty economics show just how fiercely both carriers guard their Chicago customer base. Even as United executives have pushed back against oversimplified narratives that airline profits come effortlessly from credit cards alone, pointing to the real operational cost of carrying award travelers, both United and American treat Chicago loyalty as too valuable to surrender lightly. In this light, concourse gates are the door to a much bigger prize: long-term brand security among Chicago's flyers.

What began as a dispute over departure-share gate formulas has become a test of endurance where courtroom rulings, federal scheduling caps, and loyalty economics converge at Chicago O'Hare. United and American are each fighting to protect a hub that anchors regional connectivity and high-value cardholder engagement, even as aggressive schedule padding runs headlong into physical runway and construction limits. Neither carrier can afford to treat O'Hare as expendable territory when hub scale directly shapes both flight reliability and long-term customer retention.

The FAA scheduling limits extension runs through October 30, 2027; subsequent appellate and trial proceedings following the Illinois Appellate Court's November 19, order in American Airlines v. City of Chicago (Illinois Courts), and phased ORDNext milestones such as Concourse D, Concourse E, and the Global Terminal stretching into the 2030s are landmark turning points that are upcoming. How both airlines balance disciplined schedule growth against those regulatory and construction guardrails will decide once and for all who is at the helm of O'Hare's next era.

#6196. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

Aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's new premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a new product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#6195. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

Citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

Citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

But Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

Like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

Generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points

Unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi says statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

In many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT."

If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

Citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

#6193. Hah: Emirates Puts Auditors On Flights To “Provide Support & Guidance” To Crew

Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service issues at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a new initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants…

Emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a new initiative involving this small group of employees:

On 3 November, Emirates introduced a new initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers…

A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha)

Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

It goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

When it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”

As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”

I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”

There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

Need them on Qatar Airways. Service has not been the same since the war.

Why would an auditor on board create stress? If you are doing what you are supposed to be doing, then there would not be a problem. That auditor that write up how wonderfully well you performed your duties and are ready for promotion.

I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. On those flights I wear a uniform and am additional to the crew complement and my role is to support and to a lesser degree assess member of my flying team. I find it really beneficial as airline crew are typically remote workers and rarely have access to their ground manager. It also gives me the ability to see first hand lots of the pain points my team complain to me about - service routines, galley layouts etc. I don't think these kind of roles are that unusual in the airline world. We just aren't called 'Standard Pursers' ouch.

If they're not "working" the flight, I could perceive this not going well with customers as well in a way: if you see people constantly passing by you and never checking on you, or if you ask that person for help and they direct it to another person, then it could come across the wrong way. Imagine you press the call attendant button and the Standard Purser just walks right by you. You'd probably think that you're being ignored by staff / they're slacking off.

If only all airlines had in-flight service auditors, the skies would be a better place.

#6192. Alaska Airlines Crew Reportedly Too Shaken To Fly After ICE Arrests On Seattle Jet Bridge

An Alaska Airlines pilot reportedly walked away from his aircraft during boarding on Saturday morning after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two passengers on a Seattle jet bridge. Two flight attendants were also said to be so overwhelmed by the incident that they asked to be replaced.

The arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) as passengers boarded Alaska flight AS1306 to Los Angeles, which ended up being delayed by more than three hours. Video footage of the incident, which has sparked widespread outrage, shows masked officers struggling with travelers near the aircraft door.

The incident occurred on Saturday morning as Alaska passengers were boarding a Boeing 737-800 bound for Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). Speaking to local radio station KUOW, passenger Aidan Mendoza said masked ICE agents struggled with a man and a woman on the jet bridge at Gate N9, leaving around 50 passengers pressed against the jet bridge wall.

Amid the chaos, Mendoza said an Alaska pilot walked back up the jet bridge looking uncomfortable and unsure of what to do, adding that "he didn't come back." KUOW also reports that two Alaska flight attendants were so overwhelmed that they asked to be "subbed out." Mendoza decided not to board the flight, saying a gate agent removed him from the passenger list before customer service refunded his ticket.

In a statement to Simple Flying, an Alaska spokesperson did not confirm whether any crew members had to be replaced, but said it was "not provided advance notice of the enforcement action" and is "working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred." The spokesperson added,

"We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306. We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests."

In a statement, ICE said it had launched an operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza (who is unrelated to passenger Aidan Mendoza), a Mexican national who it said had overstayed his visa. The agency claimed other travelers "began to obstruct and assault" officers during the arrest, while a second passenger, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, "hurled hot coffee on the officers." ICE said Hernandez Mejia, also from Mexico, had overstayed her visa and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

The Port of Seattle, which operates the airport, said it was "outraged" by the incident, emphasizing that immigration enforcement at SEA takes place without its involvement or knowledge. According to the Port, local federal immigration authorities had previously agreed to protocols at the airport, and it is now investigating whether any of those agreements were breached.

Saturday's arrests drew strong criticism from Washington officials, including Governor Bob Ferguson, who said ICE was "completely and totally out of control." Ferguson added that he was looking into how the agents accessed the jet bridge and whether they violated a state law prohibiting law enforcement officers, including federal immigration agents, from wearing face coverings.

Agents are even patrolling jetbridges to conduct document checks.

ICE has stepped up arrests at US airports since the summer to apprehend travelers overstaying visas. Other notable cases include a woman from Ecuador escorted off a jet bridge in Denver in July, and a Southwest Airlines flight attendant taken into custody while on the job at Nashville International Airport (BNA).

Airlines have little control over immigration enforcement at the gate. Airlines for America (A4A), which represents the largest US carriers, said in August that it was holding discussions with ICE and TSA to ensure proper procedures were in place when law enforcement activity takes place at airports.

Airline unions have been more outspoken, such as the Association of Professional Flight Attendants (APFA), which represents more than 26,000 American Airlines flight attendants. APFA recently said it was "deeply alarmed" by ICE's escalating tactics and warned it could put passengers and crew in danger.

#6191. Bilt Rent Day Promotion December 2026: JetBlue Mosaic Status Challenge

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus new ways that housing rewards are offered.

There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With a new month being right around the corner, I’d like to cover the details of the December 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a JetBlue Mosaic elite status challenge, as well as an up to 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions (which isn’t a very good deal). It’s interesting to see a second month in a row with no transfer bonus…

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

On the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:

Let me cut to the chase — don’t redeem your points this way. It’s a bad value. Ordinarily you get 0.55 cents per Bilt point for statement credit redemptions, so even with a 100% bonus, you’re looking at getting 1.1 cents per point. Hard pass.

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:

The status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:

Regardless of which tier you initially match to, the status you get to keep is based on the activity over the course of those three months. As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $100 spent on JetBlue, or every $1,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

This of course comes at a generally useful time for JetBlue elite status, given that the airline is introducing first class, with space available upgrades being an elite perk. However, it’s worth emphasizing that this really isn’t such a special offer, as it’s basically just JetBlue’s standard status match challenge offer. Except in this case, you can unlock it with Bilt elite status rather than airline elite status.

On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for December 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions, which can get you at most 1.1 cents per point of value. Please don’t redeem your points that way. JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

Washingtonians have a new option to Portugal next summer.

TAP Air Portugal will launch a new thrice-weekly service from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Porto Airport (OPO) on March 30, 2027. Westbound flights will operate on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays through the summer, and on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays beginning in October.

TAP, a Star Alliance partner of United Airlines, will fly an Airbus A321LR on the new IAD-OPO route. The long-range, single-aisle aircraft is fitted with 16 lie-flat business-class seats and 155 economy seats.

The new Portugal route is the latest international addition at IAD. United plans to launch new service to Toulouse, France, in April and to Milan in May, using its new long-range A321XLR on the former route.

International seats from IAD will increase nearly 7% in the first six months of 2027 compared to this year, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

IAD is undergoing a massive, $22 billion redevelopment to bring its infrastructure up to modern standards. The first piece — a 14-gate section of the new Concourse E that includes a new, large United Club — opened earlier in November. Future phases include a new international arrivals facility that would support additional long-haul growth.

And if the redevelopment plan stays on schedule, IAD could retire its jet-age mobile lounges by the mid-2030s.

TAP’s new OPO route complements its existing service to IAD from Lisbon Airport (LIS).

The state-owned Portuguese airline is in the process of being privatized as part of the Lufthansa Group. The German airline conglomerate plans to buy an initial 44.9% stake in TAP, aiming to close the deal by the first quarter of 2028.

Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx said in October that once the TAP deal is done, Lufthansa intends to integrate the Portuguese airline into its transatlantic joint venture with Air Canada and United.

#6189. The Rise & Fall Of The World’s First Commercial Jetliner

Manufactured from 1949 to 1964, the de Havilland DH.106 Comet was the world's first commercial jet airliner. It was powered by four jet engines and included a pressurized cabin. The engines were built into the wing roots, giving it a distinct, aerodynamically sleek appearance.

The jet rose to enormous historical significance for the entire aviation industry and was also the high watermark for British commercial aviation. Yet the Comet's success was short-lived. Its design made it prone to metal fatigue after repeated pressurization. Two early fatal hull losses permanently damaged its market position.

The idea for a British jet airliner was born during the Second World War. The Brabazon Committee recommended developing and producing a pressurized, nonstop transatlantic mail aircraft that could carry a 2,200 lb (1,000 kg) payload. The conventional wisdom at the time was that jet engines were not fuel efficient or reliable enough for transatlantic flight. De Havilland head Sir Geoffrey de Havilland used his influence to propose that there should be a specification for a turbojet-powered design.

The Brabazon Committee awarded a contract to de Havilland to produce its Type 106, initially considered a small, short-range jet aircraft, while other manufacturers were also commissioned for other designs. The Type 106 featured untested elements and was financially risky, but the British Overseas Airways Corporation (BOAC) placed an order for 10 aircraft.

De Havilland put together a design team to create the aircraft, which was led by Ronald Bishop, the brain behind the Mosquito fighter-bomber. The initial concept was for an unconventional tailless design. However, BOAC's demand to increase capacity from 24 to 36 seats forced the designers to opt for something more conventional. The final version was named DH.106 Comet in December 1947. First orders were then completed, with both BOAC and British South American Airways invested. They committed to 14 aircraft, to be delivered by 1952.

The first Comet prototype was ready in 1949. On its maiden flight, the jet took off from Hatfield Aerodrome and flew for 31 minutes. John "Cats Eyes" Cunningham, a former RAF night-fighter pilot, was at the controls. The second prototype, G-ALZK, was registered in July 1950 and amassed 500 flying hours. Qantas sent its experts to observe its operations.

The first production aircraft was G-ALYP, nicknamed "Yoke Peter", which first flew on January 9, 1951. The jet completed the world's first jetliner flight with paying passengers. It flew from London to Johannesburg. By September 1952, all the aircraft in BOAC's initial order had arrived. G-ALYZ was the last to be delivered, carrying cargo on South American routes according to simulated passenger schedules. On August 4, 1952, Prince Philip returned from the Helsinki Olympic Games on the aircraft.

The table below uses BAE Systems data to show the specifications for the Comet 1:

4 x De Havilland Ghost 50 engines producing 4,450 lbf each

Early Comet operations showed its viability in commercial operations. It carried 30,000 passengers and was profitable on flights with a load factor as low as 43%. The jet also greatly outperformed its piston-engined rivals. The jet flew 55% faster, and its faster climb rate cut flight time.

Popular Mechanics magazine wrote in 1952 that the Comet was between three and five years ahead of any other proposed jet aircraft. Writer Aubrey Cookman rode the aircraft on a mammoth six-stop trip from London to Johannesburg. "Scheduled eight-mile-a-minute travel in the stratosphere is here. I did it, and from now on so can you," Cookman begins. "Regular airline life insurance was available at the usual rate and I suspect a few snapped it up," they later admitted.

The trip took 17 hours and 16 minutes, but was still about twice as fast as contemporary piston aircraft. These multi-stop odysseys were typical in the Comet's first years of operation. In the summer of 1953, eight Comets left London per week, with the destinations being Johannesburg, Tokyo, Singapore and Colombo. The Tokyo flight took 36 hours, with the same trip on BOAC's DC-4M-4 Argonaut taking over 86 hours.

The table below shows the fleet sizes of the Comet's most significant operators in the 1960s, using data collected by Simple Flying:

From 1953, several other airlines placed orders for the Comet. Union Aéromaritime de Transport and Air France both ordered three Comet 1As, which had greater fuel capacity. De Havilland also developed the Comet 2, which had better engines and was longer. Air India, British Commonwealth Pacific Airlines, Japan Airlines and more made orders, although Qantas concluded that the Comet wasn't yet ready for its London to Canberra route.

Across its service, the Comet was involved in 25 hull-loss accidents, 13 of which were fatal, leading to the tragic deaths of 492 people, according to Aviation Safety Network. That is 22% of all airframes built. The first accident came on October 26, 1952. BOAC Flight 115 was attempting to take off from Rome Ciampino G. B. Pastine Airport (CIA) when it failed to get airborne. It ran into rough ground at the end of the airport. Just two passengers suffered minor injuries, but the aircraft never flew again.

A new Canadian Pacific Airlines Comet 1A suffered a similar accident in March 1953, resulting in the deaths of five crew and six passengers. It was the first fatal jetliner crash. The first airborne fatal jetliner crash occurred on May 2, 1953. BOAC Flight 783 crashed in a thunderstorm shortly after takeoff from Calcutta-Dum Dum Airport (CCU). The jet was seen hurtling towards the ground with no wings. All 43 people on board died.

The following year saw the notorious Comet disasters of 1954. These were BOAC Flight 781 and South African Airways Flight 201. Flight 781 was the most deadly, with the aircraft breaking up in midair 20 minutes after takeoff from Ciampino.

Pan Am's Boeing 747SP featured luxurious cabins and dining, reinforcing its legacy.

"The cost of solving the Comet mystery must be reckoned neither in money nor in manpower," said British Prime Minister Winston Churchill. The Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough led an investigation into the accidents. Its work showed that cabin pressurization cycles had caused metal fatigue cracks. The stress had been concentrated near windows and hatch corners, as well as around the automatic direction-finding (ADF) antenna cutout. These small areas of fatigue were sufficient to cause the thin-skinned fuselage to fail, leading the aircraft to break up in midair with deadly consequences.

The findings resulted in the Comet 1 fleet being grounded in 1954. Future Comet iterations, like the Comet 4, had thicker skin, and areas prone to stress were also targeted. De Havilland completed a refit program to strengthen the skin and wing structure of existing aircraft and install rounder windows.

The Comet 4 first flew in April 1958, marking the Comet's return to service. Comet 3 customers canceled their orders and switched to the newer iteration, which had improved fuel capacity. BOAC used the jet for regular services from London to New York, completing the trip in an incredibly short six hours and 12 minutes. It was the first jetliner to make a nonstop transatlantic trip. Yetat this time, the Boeing 707 was coming into service, as was the Douglas DC-8. These American aircraft were larger, faster, and had a better range. The days of Britain dominating jet aviation were numbered.

A Dan-Air Comet (pictured above) performed the final flight of the world's first commercial jet aircraft on November 9, 1980. The British carrier flew nearly 50 Comets, usually acquiring them secondhand during the 1960s and 1970s, with three Comet variants in the fleet. The final flight saw a Comet 4C take off from London Gatwick Airport (LGW). The plane then made a low pass at London Heathrow Airport (LHR) before making another low pass at RAF Brize Norton. The destination honored G-BDIW's former owner, the RAF, where it was registered as XR398.

The passengers received certificates showing they had been on the last flight. The jet then traveled on to Germany for preservation at the Flugausstellung Peter Junior museum in Hermeskeil. The service was not the last time that a Comet took to the skies. The UK Ministry of Technology continued to use the jet to research avionics, radar, and radio-based technology. That aircraft, XS235, continued these duties until its final retirement in March 1997. It concluded 45 years of the Comet being seen over skies in Britain and around the world. The plane is now part of the Cold War Jets Collection at Bruntingthorpe Aerodrome in Leicestershire.
