#6172. Airbus Now Has 3 Final Assembly Lines In Alabama & Only One Of Them Builds A220s

At its manufacturing campus in Mobile, Alabama, Airbus now operates three final assembly lines, two dedicated to the A320 Family and only one building the A220, following the October 13, 2025 inauguration of its second A320 final assembly line. That two-to-one split is a key point of note in the growth of Airbus' Gulf Coast operations, but it also makes many wonder about how the manufacturer balances high-volume single-aisle demand against regional to small narrowbody production on US soil.

Why allocate two final assembly lines in Alabama to the A320 Family and keep just one line on the A220? This article looks at how the Mobile site has evolved alongside trade dynamics, global production targets, and American airline orders, demonstrating how Airbus is positioning domestic assembly to serve a massive US backlog and keep tariff and supply-chain risks in check.

Airbus' manufacturing campus at Mobile Aeroplex at Brookley in Alabama began commercial aircraft assembly in 2015 with a single A320 final assembly line, establishing its first commercial production foothold in the United States. Four years later, in 2019, Airbus added a dedicated A220 final assembly line alongside the existing A320 operation, and the first Mobile-built A220 was delivered to Delta Air Lines in October 2020. That phased buildout expanded the site into a multi-line narrowbody hub before reaching a new milestone on October 13, 2025, when Airbus inaugurated its second A320 final assembly line, bringing the campus to three final assembly lines in total, with two building the A320 Family and one building the A220.

The October 2025 expansion added about 350,000 square feet (3,251 square meters) of manufacturing, office, and logistics space along with roughly 1,000 additional jobs, as noted by Made In Alabama. Across the campus, the buildout incorporated more than a million square feet (more than 92,000 square meters) of A320 double-bay hangars and quad-bay hangars dedicated to the A220. With the new A320 line up and ready, the Mobile facility now spans more than 2.5 million square feet (232,257 square meters) and supports a workforce of more than 2,000 employees.

Taken together, a decade of additions took that single-line Alabama plant to a large-scale industrial complex capable of housing three distinct final assembly lines under one roof. Having double-bay and quad-bay hangars alongside 2.5 million square feet (232,257 square meters) of operational space gives the site the scale needed to run parallel single-aisle production flows without crowding earlier assembly bays.

The existence of an A220 final assembly line in Mobile traces directly back to the 2017 trade dispute in which Boeing filed a complaint against Bombardier over the C Series program, triggering steep proposed US import tariffs on Canadian-built aircraft, as reported by Business Insider. Rather than letting tariff threats shut US customers out of the program, Airbus stepped in to take control of the C Series, later rebranded as the A220, and brought final assembly onto American soil in Alabama. Building A220 airframes domestically gave US carriers a pathway to take delivery without running into cross-border trade barriers.

Assembling A220s in Alabama also gave Airbus an industrial hedge alongside its main A220 final assembly line in Mirabel, Quebec, making Mobile and Mirabel the only two final assembly sites for the aircraft type. Even after trade duties were ultimately overturned, locating domestic final assembly in the United States supported the program within a core commercial market and gave a shield to US deliveries from future trade friction.

For Airbus, having both Canadian production in Mirabel and an Alabama assembly line quickly became a permanent strategic asset. The existence of US-built A220 capability lets Airbus serve American-based airlines from inside the tariff wall while keeping the program closely integrated across North America.

The manufacturer is expanding its production capabilities.

Bringing a second A320 final assembly line online in Mobile tilts the site's narrowbody production mix decisively toward the A320 Family, giving Airbus two dedicated A320 lines against a single line for the A220. Ultimately, the A320 Family sits at the core of narrowbody airline fleet plans, so adding a second domestic assembly line expands how many single-aisle aircraft Airbus can finish in the United States and not have to rely solely on overseas final assembly plants.

For domestic customers, doubling A320 final assembly capacity in Alabama shortens the logistical path between factory completion and airline entry into service. In a different scenario, airlines would be competing exclusively for overseas build slots or shipping finished narrowbodies across the Atlantic, whereas with this added capacity, customers gain more domestic throughput on a proven aircraft family that is focused on main cabin and short to medium-haul networks.

At the same time, running two A320 lines alongside one A220 line reflects clear operational specialization rather than placing equal volume across every aircraft type. Now concentrating twin final assembly lines on the A320 Family in Mobile while keeping A220 final assembly at a single line there, Airbus matches its layout to the much larger commercial scale of A320 Family demand that has been lying overhead.

Globally, Airbus has set its sights on reaching a production rate of 75 A320 Family aircraft per month in 2027, while targeting 14 A220 aircraft per month across its Mobile and Mirabel final assembly network in 2026. Pairing two A320 final assembly lines with a single A220 line in Mobile mirrors how sharply production scale diverges between the two programs. On one hand, the A320 Family carries massive global volume requirements, whereas the A220 ramps up across a smaller single-aisle tier.

Pacing a single A220 final assembly line alongside two A320 lines also highlights how industrial delays govern real-world delivery speed. Even when final assembly bays are in the right place, hitting monthly targets depends on keeping major components, such as engines, cabin interiors, and aerostructures, flowing smoothly from global suppliers into each assembly station. Any lag in component deliveries or line-side tooling can slow how quickly a single line or a dual-line setup turns out completed jets.

For Airbus' wider manufacturing network, keeping the A220 on one Mobile line while scaling A320 Family output toward rate 75 is an exercise in calibrated pacing. Over-allocating floor space to lower-volume builds would slow down the overall production rate, so instead Airbus paces each program according to its production curve and supply-chain readiness, meaning global delivery commitments stay aligned with factory capacity.

Do Airbus or Embraer's narrow-bodied airlines dominate the short-haul and regional market?

With more than 850 Airbus aircraft on order for US customers, as per Airbus data, domestic airline demand provides the commercial helping hand behind expanding final assembly capacity in Alabama. American carriers rely heavily on single-aisle jets to refresh aging fleets, grow regional and mainline networks, and support long-term fleet modernization across both major network airlines and low-cost operators. Having deep domestic order books gives Airbus strong visibility into steady US delivery pull over the coming years.

Against that backdrop, Airbus' bigger ambition is for US carriers' narrowbodies to eventually come from Mobile and not still be reliant on imported airframes. Aligning Alabama final assembly with American airline demand brings production closer to the end customer, helping streamline handovers, acceptance flights, and customer support across the United States. Even with only one line dedicated to the A220 alongside two A320 Family lines, domestic assembly positions Mobile as the centerpiece of Airbus' US narrowbody delivery strategy.

Turning that long-term goal into everyday reality still depends on matching build mix and slot availability to what US airlines actually need next. Because carrier order books span multiple single-aisle sizes and delivery windows, Mobile's configuration plays a central role in how quickly Airbus can turn US backlog commitments into active aircraft on American flight lines.

Mobile was once just a single-line narrowbody operation, and now, it has evolved into a deliberate two-to-one industrial split. Two A320 Family final assembly lines alongside one A220 line are designed to balance high-volume single-aisle scale with tariff-resilient domestic flexibility. Now committing its A220 production in Alabama after the 2017 trade dispute and expanding A320 assembly capacity in October 2025, Airbus has positioned its Gulf Coast campus to serve United States airline demand closer to home while keeping supply-chain pacing and cabin brand expectations aligned.

Looking ahead, the clearest benchmark for this strategy is how Mobile and the wider manufacturing network work together through the end of 2027, when Airbus aims to reach a monthly production rate of 70 to 75 A320 Family aircraft and stabilize at a rate of 75 alongside its ongoing A220 ramp-up and domestic backlog deliveries. Hitting those volume milestones and not straining supplier flow or sacrificing cabin consistency will show whether a two-line A320 and one-line A220 footprint in Alabama becomes the status quo going forward for Airbus' next decade in the United States.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Surprisingly, while Tianjin and Mobile second FALs were both inaugurated in October 2025, only Tianjin's has started delivering planes, with a first A320neo in September 2026

#6171. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6170. Buy Southwest Rapid Rewards Points For 50% Off (1.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

Looking to buy Southwest points? Rapid Rewards is currently offering up to a 50% discount on purchased points, which is an opportunity to acquire them for just 1.5 cents each. Is that a good deal?

While there has long been value in strategically buying points, the concept of a revenue based frequent flyer program selling points can be tougher to rationalize. So that I don’t bury the lede, let me say that I’d only buy points in a very narrow set of circumstances, like if trying to top off a points balance for a specific redemption.

Link: Buy Southwest Rapid Rewards points with this promotion for 50% off

Between 12:01AM CT on November 19 and 11:59PM CT on December 31, 2026, Southwest Rapid Rewards is offering a discount on purchased points. With Southwest, it’s common for different members to be eligible for different offers, so you’ll have to log into your Rapid Rewards account to see what you’re eligible for.

However, the best version of the offer to buy Southwest points provides up to a 50% discount, structured as follows:

Ordinarily you can buy Southwest points for 3.0 cents each, and that price is inclusive of the 7.5% federal excise tax. Given the limit of being able to purchase up to 100,000 Rapid Rewards points per day, that means if you maxed out this promotion, you could buy 100,000 points for $1,500, which is a cost of 1.5 cents per point.

Southwest sells points in increments of 1,000 points, with 2,000 points being the minimum. Ordinarily there’s a daily maximum of buying 60,000 points, but during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 100,000 points.

Just in the interest of being thorough, some Rapid Rewards members may be eligible for smaller percentage discounts, so let me crunch the numbers on those potential offers:

Southwest has no annual limit on how many Rapid Rewards points you can buy. The only restriction is that you can ordinarily buy at most 60,000 points per calendar day. During this promotion, that cap has been increased to 100,000 points, though.

Note that the purchase of Southwest points is non-refundable, and buying Southwest points doesn’t count toward Rapid Rewards elite status or Companion Pass qualification. Purchased points typically post nearly instantly, but in some cases, it can take up to 72 hours for them to post.

Southwest Rapid Rewards frequently offers promotions on purchasing points. When the program does have a buy points promotion, the 50% discount offer is pretty standard. So I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a relatively immediate use for redeeming them, rather than anything else.

Below is a chart with some of the recent Southwest buy points promotions that we’ve seen, before this one.

If you’d like to buy Southwest Airlines points, note that purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore this wouldn’t be treated as a Southwest purchase if you’re using a Rapid Rewards credit card.

I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue based frequent flyer program, and the number of points required for a flight is roughly correlated to the revenue cost of a flight. However, there is a dynamic element to the pricing, whereby the value you get per point varies significantly, based on the flight and fare class you redeem for. With this, we’re seeing redemption values as low as 1.1 cents per point, and as high as 1.5 cents per point, give or take.

As you can tell, there are probably few situations where it makes sense to buy points for 1.5 cents (or more) each, when they can’t be redeemed for that, best case scenario.

Let me cut to the chase — there are few situations where it makes sense to purchase Rapid Rewards points. Even at the discounted cost, there’s not usually value in buying points for 1.5 cents each when you can typically only redeem them for less than that. So don’t buy these points speculatively, unless you know exactly what you’re doing, and have a redemption in mind.

There are three potential scenarios I’d like to address, including the main scenario where I think it could make sense (but not really), which is to build up a balance of Southwest points, given the flexibility this provides.

Some might buy Rapid Rewards points in order to top off their account so they have enough points for a Rapid Rewards award ticket. I guess this might be worth it to some if you need a small number of points, though personally I’d just keep collecting points and then redeem with your next ticket.

The Southwest Airlines Companion Pass is one of the best values in domestic travel. If you qualify for this, you can always have a companion travel with you for just the standard taxes, regardless of whether you’re booking a cash ticket or redeeming points.

For those with a Companion Pass, buying Southwest points could get you outsized value:

However, there’s still absolutely zero reason to do that. You’d be better off just booking a paid ticket and then having a companion fly with you.

There is one major benefit in general to paying for a ticket with Southwest Rapid Rewards points rather than cash. While Southwest Airlines has no change fees on both revenue and award tickets on most kinds of fares:

I do think there’s big value in having a stash of Rapid Rewards points. I use this when I speculatively want to book travel (including for friends and family), since there’s no downside.

If you’re looking to earn Southwest points, there are plenty of ways to rack up this currency with credit card rewards:

On top of that, Rapid Rewards has a variety of co-branded Chase credit cards, which can be a great way to rack up rewards. This includes cards like the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more), etc.

Through December 31, 2026, Southwest is selling Rapid Rewards points with a discount of up to 50%, which brings the cost down to as little as 1.5 cents per point. I still don’t think there are many circumstances under which it makes sense to buy points, given that Rapid Rewards is a revenue based frequent flyer program, and points can typically only be redeemed for 1.1-1.5 cents each toward the cost of a ticket.

Under what circumstances do you think it’s worth buying Southwest Airlines points?

#6169. These 14 apps and websites make award redemptions easier to find

Learn how to get started earning and redeeming rewards so you can make the most of your everyday spending.

See how far your points, miles and dollars go in TPG's first loyalty report.

See how TPG ranks the top US airlines for 2026.

As a senior writer for TPG, Tarah Chieffi helps readers travel better, more often and within their budget.

Mackenzie Roche is an editor on TPG’s content operations team. She previously worked for three years as a travel editor at U.S. News & World Report.

We get it — mastering points and miles is no easy feat. You may have seen our guide to getting started with points and miles, but what happens once you're ready to cash those points in for a trip?

Maximizing points and miles to travel luxuriously without breaking the bank doesn’t need to be laborious and time-consuming. In fact, there are various tools available that make it easier to find hotel and flight award availability.

With these tools, you can use your points to travel where you want, when you want and how you want in 2027 (and beyond) without spending hours searching for availability.

Here are 14 of the best apps and websites that make award travel redemptions easier and less stressful.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: The basic plan is free, but you really unlock the best features with a paid membership. Right now, TPG has a special offer: Roame.travel is offering TPG readers 40% off the Friends of Roame Pro membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY," which brings the regular price down to $94 per year (from $156).

When you sign up for a free Roame account, you can search more than 25 airline programs for instant, real-time award availability.

After clicking a flight option, you can see the points required to book, as well as the available transfer partners and recommended credit cards to help you earn the points you need. You can even add your existing credit cards to your virtual wallet to get recommendations.

With a paid membership, you can also track points pricing with route alerts.

As always, we recommend confirming award availability before transferring points.

Related: The complete guide to searching award space on Roame.travel

What it does: Helps travelers find airline award space.

What it costs: There is a free version that alerts you to seat availability on a specific flight, but you can get additional alerts and better search functions with the Basic ($6.99 per month), Premium ($12.99 per month) or Elite ($19.99 per month) membership options. There are discounts if you choose to pay annually.

And there's an ExpertFlyer discount exclusively for TPG readers: New users can get 30% off any annual subscription.

ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG's parent company, Red Ventures) is a helpful tool for viewing airline schedules, seat maps and flight statuses across more than 400 airlines, as well as award and upgrade availability on select carriers. You can set seat alerts to help snag your preferred seat if it isn't available when you book your flight.

Related: How to use ExpertFlyer alerts to snag a better seat

A free account lets you set one alert at a time, but you will need a Basic, Premium or Elite membership to run an award search. Once you are logged in with a paid account, you can search using the "Awards & Upgrades" tab. When you enter your travel details and select the airline you'd like to fly, you'll see the fare classes that ExpertFlyer can search alongside a description.

When you click the search button at the bottom of the screen, ExpertFlyer presents you with a list of the available flights broken down by date. Once you have the date, flight number and fare class, you can book your flight online or by calling the airline directly. If the flight you're looking to book doesn't have seats available in your preferred fare class, you can set an alert, and ExpertFlyer will email you if a seat is released, taking the legwork out of award searches.

ExpertFlyer's expanded Systemwide Upgrades feature lets American Airlines elite members with systemwide upgrades search availability up to 330 days out across multiple regions. This feature is only available with ExpertFlyer's Elite plan. Basic and Premium members can still search systemwide upgrade space one route at a time through the “Awards & Upgrades” tab.

What it does: Tracks hotel award availability at Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties.

What it costs: Free for basic membership; $3.99 per month for a Gold membership and $7.99 per month for a Platinum membership (though there's a 40% off Thanksgiving promotion if you elect to pay annually).

MaxMyPoint is a website that lets you check award availability for Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties worldwide. It takes the guesswork out of award redemption searches by showing real-time award pricing and availability.

The homepage shows popular properties, but you can filter by hotel brand, location, price and more to narrow down your results. You can also search date-based deals or use the map search feature to search multiple hotels in a single destination.

Once you choose a property, you can view a calendar that displays available points pricing and the lowest cash rate. This allows you to plan your trip around the dates with the best points pricing.

After you select your check-in date, you’ll automatically be redirected to the property’s website to start the booking process. If you can’t find the availability you are looking for, you can register for a free account and set up an alert to receive an email if availability changes.

Paid memberships come with additional features, including more frequent and more detailed alerts.

What it does: Displays award pricing in Google Flights.

What it costs: Free for a standard plan, $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year for a Pro plan. If you want to pay annually, there's also a paid option for alerts only, which costs $34.99 per year.

Points Path is a browser extension that displays award pricing alongside cash prices for select airlines in Google Flights. The free version includes points versus cash pricing for Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue and United Airlines.

It also tells you which transferable points can be used with the airlines it supports, as well as when to book at a paid rate or with points. Once you select an itinerary, you can book it directly with the airline using points or cash, as you would with Google Flights.

Related: How to use the Points Path extension to compare cash and award rates in Google Flights

Points Path simplifies the decision of when to use cash or miles to buy airline tickets. Points Path Pro unlocks additional features such as price alerts, access to additional airline programs and customizable points valuations.

The browser extension is compatible with Chrome, Safari, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Brave and Arc.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: There is a free version, but for real-time availability, you can purchase a Standard ($10.75 per month) or Premium ($21.67 per month) membership. These discounts are available when you pay annually. Concierge services are available starting at $200 per passenger.

TPG readers get seven months free on Standard Annual membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY7."

Point.me's robust interface searches for award flights across more than 30 loyalty programs and more than 150 airlines.

By entering your itinerary details, Point.me will display award availability, including which transfer partner offers the most value for your buck.

In addition to the free and paid versions, you can book one-on-one sessions with one of Point.me's expert consultants who can assist you with flight bookings, points strategies, elite status and mileage runs and more.

American Express cardholders can access a limited version of Point.me for free. As with the full version, you can search for award flight availability, but you will only see results from Amex transfer partners. This is a good way to try Point.me for free if you have Membership Rewards points that you want to transfer to an airline loyalty program to purchase tickets.

What it does: Helps you maximize your points by finding the best flight redemptions.

What it costs: Free for the basic plan; $99 per year for the premium plan (but there's a current promotion for $20 off).

Pointhound takes the guesswork (and hours of searching) out of turning your points and miles into award flights. The site’s search tool helps you find the best deals by displaying preferred booking options for a designated route and date.

For example, if you search for a flight from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), Pointhound will display your flight results alongside all available booking options.

If you know you want to fly Air France but don’t have enough Flying Blue miles, you can see which programs transfer to Air France partners, including those that have current transfer bonuses.

Once you’ve chosen a route and booking option, Pointhound will walk you through the points transfer and booking process. (You still book directly through the airline; Pointhound gives you the instructions on how to do it.)

If you want to stay informed about the latest flight deals, you can sign up to receive flight alerts from specific airports via email.

What it does: Searches for real-time award flight and hotel availability.

What it costs: Free for unlimited basic searches, $19.99 per month or $119.95 per year for Premium (though there are Black Friday promotions).

PointsYeah streamlines hotel and airline award bookings by searching all major credit cards, award programs and booking portals in under 20 seconds. You can view results from more than 20 airline programs and six major hotel programs.

Once you've chosen a flight, PointsYeah will display all available booking options. If you already have enough points, you can book directly with the airline; however, PointsYeah will show the amount of points you'd need to transfer from various credit card programs, including details on current transfer bonuses.

You can create flight and hotel alerts. Basic accounts get up to four flight and hotel price alerts, as well as five multi-region alerts for a 30-day search window.

Premium members get up to 32 flight alerts, 30 hotel alerts and up to 150 multi-region alerts for a 90-day search window. When you upgrade to Premium, you also get access to United Airlines upgrade alerts, expanded date and destination availability when you search and the ability to set custom values for your points currencies.

What it does: Provides real-time search results across multiple airports and travel dates simultaneously.

What it costs: Free for the basic plan; $12.99 per month or $109.99 per year for AwardTool Pro (with Black Friday discounts available).

If your travel dates and destinations are flexible, AwardTool can display results for multiple flights in a single search. If you're extra flexible, you can utilize the Panorama feature to view award pricing by region rather than a specific destination or the Deals feature to see the best award rates from your chosen airport to anywhere in the world.

When you upgrade to AwardTool Pro, you unlock access to additional and expanded search capabilities, up to 100 award alerts, unlimited Panorama alerts and live seat map availability.

What it does: Gondola helps you find the best hotel deals and use your points to book.

Gondola is a free AI-powered hotel booking tool that tracks your points and miles balances to help you maximize your rewards. When you search for your travel dates and destination, the results will display cash and points pricing, along with ratings to help you determine which is the better value.

You'll see results from major hotel groups like Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Accor and more.

Once you've chosen a property, Gondola will direct you to the hotel's website to book award stays directly with the hotel. For paid reservations, Gondola will book the hotel on your behalf, allowing you to earn the usual points and elite benefits, along with between 3% and 7% cash back in the form of Gondola Cashback for every stay.

Gondola will also monitor your bookings and alert you if the price drops, so you can rebook at the lower price.

What it does: Checks flight award availability based on your itinerary and preferred airline.

What it costs: Free for five economy award availability searches per day; $3.39 per month for a Premium subscription or $9.99 per month for a First Class subscription, with discounts for annual payments.

SeatSpy is an easy-to-use website that checks award availability across 10 airlines, most of which are not U.S.-based carriers.

Select your airline, departure and end destination airports, then hit “Search” to see availability across the next 12 months.

SeatSpy is free to use if you’re only searching for economy availability. Where the product really shines, however, is in its premium subscriptions.

The entry-level subscription, Premium, allows unlimited searches across all fares and up to four active alerts sent via email, WhatsApp and Telegram. It also includes AwardWallet integration, so you can track how many points you have to redeem.

First Class includes everything in the Premium plan, plus unlimited alerts sent instantly instead of hourly, along with SMS alerts and "experience alerts."

Both subscriptions offer a “Where Can I Go” search feature that shows all destinations with award availability from your departure airport on the travel dates you select.

It may have few features when compared to other services on this list, but in terms of simplicity, it’s a great site — especially if you’re looking at Europe-based airlines.

What it does: Displays award seat availability on domestic and international flights across fare classes.

What it costs: Free for the basic version and $12.99 monthly for the Pro version, which includes Rooms.aero access for hotel award searches.

Seats.aero regularly refreshes award space across dozens of airline programs and provides results for the next month or two.

The Pro version allows you to search up to a year in advance, set up unlimited alerts (whereas free users get only five) and receive SMS notifications when award availability turns up.

Related: How I use Seats.aero every day to find the best airline award availability in seconds

What it does: Displays hotel award availability across several major hotel brands.

What it costs: Free for the basic version; if you want the paid Pro version, you can get it through your Seats.aero membership.

Rooms.aero works similarly to its counterpart, Seats.aero. Users can search seven major hotel programs — Choice Privileges, Hilton Honors, World of Hyatt, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, I Prefer Hotel Rewards and Wyndham Rewards — for hotel award availability across certain dates or destinations.

Related: How to use Rooms.aero to find the best hotel award availability

Rooms.aero uses a valuation system to indicate whether you are getting good, average or poor value for your points for a given redemption. You can also filter by points program and the maximum number of points per night. When you choose a hotel, you'll see a calendar view with points and cash rates.

You can also use Rooms.aero to set availability alerts to notify you when a specific hotel or destination has points availability. With a Pro account, you get access to advanced search filters, SMS alerts and more.

What it does: Displays points, miles and cash pricing for flights and hotels.

What it costs: Free for a basic membership; $14.99 for a one-time “Trip Pass” valid for three days; and $12.50 per month (or $150 annually) for a premium membership.

Awayz helps you make the most of your hard-earned points and miles by showing when to redeem points and when to pay cash. You can use the Awayz search tool to find specific flight routes or hotels in specific destinations. Awayz will then display live award availability and cash rates so you can make a side-by-side comparison.

You can use the site’s robust filtering system to display certain hotel chains, transferable award programs and even those that qualify for free night certificates.

For flights, you can filter to see only certain airlines, choose the time of day you’d prefer to travel and even indicate which aircraft type you’d prefer. You can also update your “wallet” with the credit cards and reward balances you currently have, so it can tailor your results further.

Related: How to use Awayz to improve your hotel award searches

A free membership includes five hotel and five airline searches per month. An Awayz Trip Pass (great for one-time planning) includes 50 hotel searches, 50 flight searches and 10 award availability alerts for a one-time fee of $14.99. An Awayz Premium membership includes 500 hotel searches, 100 flight searches and 30 award availability alerts, among other perks.

What it does: Finds flight schedules and prices, with several filtering options, for most major airlines.

Google Flights is your one-stop shop for finding the best flight for your schedule and budget.

You can search flight schedules and pricing across most major airlines and sort results based on price, duration, number of stops, fare class and airlines, among other options. You can also set flight price alerts.

One of the best tools within Google Flights is Google Flights Explore.

Google Flights Explore lets you enter only your departure city, then use the interactive map to choose your destination based on current pricing.

Google Flights does not display points pricing (unless you use the Points Path plugin we mentioned earlier in this article), but that doesn’t mean it can’t help you find award space. You’ll still have to book directly through the airline, but you can save valuable search time by narrowing down your options through Google Flights first.

For example, if you have a bank of points and miles with a Star Alliance, Oneworld or SkyTeam partner airline, you can filter search results by alliance to see routing options. Or, you may find a nearby airport with better pricing that you wouldn’t have searched for otherwise.

The great thing about all these tools is that you can use them together to find award flights and free hotel nights.

No matter which combination of sites and apps you use, you’ll find that they take the guesswork out of award redemptions and put you on the fast track to becoming an expert in redeeming points and miles for your 2027 travels.

#6167. Amex Blue Cash Preferred Review: A Top Cash Back Card For Everyday Purchases

If you spend a lot at supermarkets and want to earn cash back, the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is hard to beat. The card offers 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets and on select streaming subscriptions, which can add up fast for families and anyone with a few monthly subscriptions.

In this post, I’ll cover the welcome offer, the bonus categories and how they work, the Disney streaming credit, and how this card compares to other options like the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express and the Citi Strata Premier® Card.

Link: Learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express

Before I get into the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card review, here’s a quick look at the most important features and fees:

And here are my thoughts on the main pros and cons of the Blue Cash Preferred Card:

When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, the eligibility, and the fees, are major considerations, given that they can be the first factors that impact interest in a card. So along those lines, let’s take a look at those details for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred is currently offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $300 cash back after spending $3,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

That’s a solid bonus for a card at this price point, and the six month window gives you plenty of time to hit the spending requirement. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. A few rules to know:

As you can see, this card is marketed as offering a bonus “as high as” a certain amount. The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. (Rates & Fees). That puts it in line with other mid-range cards. No first year annual fee is a nice perk, as it lets you test the card and see how much value you’re getting before you commit to the ongoing fee.

If you decide the card isn’t working for you after the first year, you can always downgrade to the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday Card.

You can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost, so that their spending can help you rack up rewards.

I wouldn’t recommend using the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card outside the U.S. or for purchases in foreign currencies. The 2.7% foreign transaction fee will eat into your rewards (Rates & Fees). There are plenty of other cards with no foreign transaction fees that are better suited for international spending.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has some excellent bonus categories, especially if you spend a lot at U.S. supermarkets and on streaming. Below is a full breakdown.

This is the headline feature of the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, and it’s the single best cash back rate for U.S. supermarket spending that I’m aware of. You earn 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%). This is the only bonus category with an earning cap.

To put that in perspective, if you spend $500 a month on U.S. supermarket spending, you’d earn $360 per year in cash back from this category alone. That more than covers the $95 annual fee.

Note that supermarkets don’t include superstores, warehouse clubs (like Costco or Sam’s Club), or discount stores. If most of your grocery shopping happens at a traditional supermarket, this card is incredibly rewarding.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also offers 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming subscriptions. The list of qualifying services is quite long and includes most of the major platforms: Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, ESPN+, HBO Max, Spotify, Apple TV, Apple Music, Amazon Music Unlimited, YouTube Premium, YouTube TV, Peacock, Sling TV, and many more.

If you’re spending $50 to $100 a month across streaming services (which many households are these days), that 6% adds up nicely.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers 3% cash back on transit purchases, including taxis, ridesharing, parking, tolls, trains, and buses. If you commute by public transit or use rideshare services regularly, this is a solid bonus category.

With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you also earn 3% cash back at eligible U.S. gas stations, with no caps. Note that this doesn’t include gas purchased at superstores, supermarkets, or warehouse clubs that sell fuel.

For purchases that don’t fall into the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is the one weak spot of the card. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll want to pair this card with something that earns a better return on everyday purchases (more on that below).

With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem. It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

As is the case for any credit card, it’s also important to consider the benefits and credits offered, if any. The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a reasonable annual fee, so what are the benefits like? Well, they’re potentially pretty solid, and can help justify the annual fee…

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers up to $10 back per month ($120 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled card to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscription is subject to auto-renewal. (Enrollment required)

Another Amex Blue Cash Preferred benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also includes an introductory 0% APR offer that can give you some breathing room on purchases and balance transfers.

Enjoy 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 12 months from the date of account opening. After that, your APR will be a variable APR of 19.74% - 28.74%

This could be helpful if you need to transfer an existing credit card balance and have some time to pay it off before interest kicks in, or if you need some extra time to pay off a big upcoming purchase. Just make sure you pay off your balance in full before the intro period ends, or you’ll be on the hook for interest after all.

One benefit that doesn’t get enough attention is the Amex Offers program. This gives you access to targeted deals with a variety of retailers, just by registering your card and making an eligible purchase.

Different Amex cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards in your wallet means more chances to save. Across my Amex cards, this program saves me hundreds of dollars per year.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card has fewer travel protections than more premium Amex cards, but it does come with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card offers the following benefits when you shop with the card:

These are all helpful benefits that you hopefully won’t have to use (though they do provide some peace of mind). Just remember you need to purchase the relevant items with your card to get this coverage.

Purchase Protection is an embedded benefit of your Card Membership and requires no enrollment. It can help protect Covered Purchases made on your Eligible Card when they’re accidentally damaged, stolen, or lost, for up to 90 days from the Covered Purchase date. The coverage is limited to up to $10,000 per occurrence, up to $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Coverage Limits Apply. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. When an American Express® Card Member charges a Covered Purchase to an Eligible Card, Extended Warranty§ can provide up to one extra year added to the Original Manufacturer’s Warranty. Applies to warranties of five (5) years or less. Coverage is up to the actual amount charged to your Card for the item up to a maximum of $10,000; not to exceed $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

I tend to lean toward points-earning cards for my own spending, but I totally get why a lot of people prefer cash back. It’s simple, flexible, and you can spend it however you want, including on travel. For that crowd, the Blue Cash Preferred is one of the best options out there.

If you’re someone who is looking to earn cash back and spends a lot at supermarkets, then the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card is an exceptional choice, in my opinion — 6% cash back will add up quickly.

The 6% cash back on streaming, and 3% cash back on transit and gas stations, will add up quickly as well, and up to $120 Disney streaming credit could be worth more than the annual fee.

However, this isn’t the card I would be using for your everyday spending, as you’d only earn 1% cash back in the categories that aren’t eligible for bonuses. So I’d acquire this card specifically with the intent of using it in the categories offering bonuses.

So, let’s take a look at what other cards you should potentially be considering.

If you like the idea of an Amex cash back card but aren’t sure about paying an annual fee, the Blue Cash Everyday Card from American Express (learn more) is the no annual fee alternative where you can earn as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

Here’s how the two Blue Cash cards compare:

In my opinion, the Blue Cash Preferred is well worth the annual fee if you spend a meaningful amount at supermarkets. The jump from 3% to 6% on U.S. supermarkets adds up fast. If you spend $500 a month at supermarkets, that extra 3% earns you $180 more per year, which nearly doubles the annual fee.

The Blue Cash Everyday does have one unique advantage: 3% cash back on U.S. online retail purchases, which the Preferred doesn’t offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and less grocery shopping, the Everyday could actually come out ahead.

The good news is that you can always start with the Blue Cash Preferred and downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after the first year if the math doesn’t work out.

If you’re just looking for the simplest cash back credit card, it’s tough to go wrong with the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase, for a total of 2% back on every purchase. That’s a solid return on everyday spending, and you don’t have to keep track of any bonus spending categories.

If you’re deciding between the Blue Cash Preferred and a mid-range card from another issuer, the $95 annual fee Citi Strata Premier Card (learn more) is worth considering. These two cards serve pretty different purposes, but they’re at the same price point:

The Blue Cash Preferred wins on supermarkets and streaming, hands down. If those are your biggest spending categories, the Blue Cash Preferred is the better card.

The Strata Premier is the more well-rounded card overall. It earns 3x points across five major categories (dining, gas, supermarkets, airfare, hotels), has no foreign transaction fees, and its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners for potentially much more than face value. If you travel or eat out a lot, the Strata Premier likely comes out ahead.

One final card worth considering alongside the Blue Cash Preferred Card is the American Express® Gold Card (learn more). It has a significantly higher annual fee, but it’s unbeatable for earning rewards at U.S. supermarkets — you’ll earn transferable Membership Rewards points too, rather than cash back.

The Blue Cash Preferred is the best cash back card for supermarket spending, and it’s not particularly close. If groceries and streaming are a big part of your monthly budget, this card can deliver serious returns, especially with the 6% rate on both categories plus the Disney streaming credit.

The annual fee pays for itself quickly if you’re spending even a moderate amount at supermarkets. Pair it with a card like the Citi Double Cash for your non-bonused spending, and you’ve got a strong cash back setup.

Just keep in mind that the 1% rate on everyday purchases means this card works best as a specialist, not your only card. Use it where it shines, and let a flat-rate card handle the rest.

If you want to learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred Card or want to apply, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express (Rates & Fees), and Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express (Rates & Fees).

#6166. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.

#6165. Here's How Much A Boeing 737 MAX 8 Earns An Airline On A Single Day Of Flying

In 2019, Boeing 737 MAX 8 operators were losing approximately $150,000 per aircraft per day in revenue. Today, each 737 MAX 8 generates around $200,000 per day, although airlines don't publish specifics, and revenue varies widely depending on how a carrier uses the aircraft.

The revenue made by each 737 MAX 8 per day is not pure profit. It is offset by depreciation or leasing costs, as well as operational and maintenance expenses. There is also a set-up cost when an airline first brings the jet into its fleet, requiring crew training and maintenance infrastructure, varying in severity depending on the degree of pre-existing fleet commonality with the Boeing 737 family.

Airlines are reluctant to publish exact data on how much money they earn for each aircraft in their fleet. However, answering this question is uniquely possible for the 737 MAX 8 because estimates emerged during the 737 MAX crisis. Each analyst had their own estimates at this time. IBA estimated total lost earnings of $150,000 per day. The Conversation reached a similar conclusion, based on three round trips a day and an average of 145 tickets sold per flight. It multiplied these sales by the US Department of Transportation average airfare in the US at the time of $343.28.

Southwest Airlines had the largest MAX fleet at the time with 34 aircraft, generating approximately $5 million in lost revenue per day. Across the entire 737 MAX fleet globally, the losses would have been closer to an eye-watering $60 million per day. This is why the crisis was so disastrous for Boeing, as there was an expectation that the manufacturer would absorb much of these costs.

IBA also notes other costs that had to be absorbed. Leasing for the jet was estimated at $360,000 a month. Staffing costs for two flight crew and four cabin crew were estimated at $5,000 per day. Airlines also had to figure out ways to adjust or increase their capacity to honor passengers' pre-existing bookings. IBA states that the cost to deal with 1,000 disrupted passengers would have been $100,000.

There are two ways that we can translate the daily revenue in 2019 into today's terms. Firstly, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics shows an average annual inflation rate of 4.27% from 2019 to 2026. That means the $150,000 of revenue per aircraft per day in 2019 is now worth $201,130.

The table below shows technical specifications for the 737 MAX 8, making use of data published by Boeing:

Another way to estimate this is to redo The Conversation's math with the current domestic itinerary fare. According to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics, this was $445.26 in the second quarter of 2026, although there is significant variation between airports. That produces an estimated daily revenue per 737 MAX 8 of $195,000, with the difference showing how air fares have not perfectly tracked the US dollar's overall inflation.

The carrier is hyperfocused on fleet simplicity and fuel efficiency for now.

As with any business, the income a 737 MAX 8 makes from ticket sales is not profit. A range of substantial costs cuts into the margins. The largest is the cost of purchasing or leasing the jet. Both Boeing and Airbus no longer formally publish list prices for their aircraft. However, the market price for a MAX 8 was $55 million in 2025, with the leasing price being $400,000 per month, both of which are comparable to the Airbus A321XLR. An aircraft fresh off the production line will be substantially more expensive than a second-hand 737 MAX 8, much like when buying a car.

The cost of buying a 737 MAX is spread across 20 to 30 years of active service rather than factored directly into daily operational costs, although depreciation over time matters when an airline decides to sell the plane. The 737 MAX promises to be around 15% to 20% more fuel-efficient than similar jets of the previous generation, meaning that operating costs are substantially lower. Furthermore, the CFM LEAP engine has proven exceptionally reliable, cutting into maintenance costs.

The table below uses data from MTU Aero Engines to show the standard specifications for the LEAP-1B engine used by the 737 MAX 8:

Some costs also have a great degree of variation between airlines. For example, airlines must invest in crew training and maintenance infrastructure to keep the jet flying. The higher the degree of commonality within the fleet, the lower the cost. For example, Southwest Airlines operates an entirely 737 fleet of over 800 aircraft, so it would have suffered relatively minor excess costs when it first introduced the 737 MAX. Other airlines for whom the 737 MAX 8 will join no other Boeing narrowbody aircraft will have to pay much more to get set up.

The reason it is so hard to nail down precise daily revenues for a 737 MAX 8 is that there is such a high degree of variation depending on how the airline uses the jet. With turnarounds under 30 minutes, some low-cost airlines can fly their 737s for between 10 and 12 hours per day. Meanwhile, legacy carriers are generally less adept at maximizing daily flight time.

In 2024, Simple Flying's Lukas Souza illustrated this factor in an article on how many flights Southwest Airlines operates with each variant of the 737 in its fleet. He used N8710M as a case study and found a great degree of variation for this single jet. On November 28, 2024, it flew just twice — from Sacramento International Airport (SMF) to Honolulu's Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL), and from HNL to Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport at Keāhole (KOA). The day before was far busier, with the itinerary broken down in the table below:

The 737 MAX's longer range and greater efficiency also mean it tends to be used differently than older 737 variants. Carriers often fly farther but with fewer flights with this jet. Varying capacity also changes revenue per flight and per day. Budget carriers pack as many passengers as possible onto every 737 MAX 8 flight, pushing the jet close to its absolute capacity of 210, while legacy carriers use premium seating at the cost of carrying fewer passengers. United Airlines configures its 737 MAX 8 with 164 or 168 seats, with significant room taken up by premium economy and economy, Seat Maps reports. Seat Maps also says that Allegiant Air crams 188 to 190 passengers into the same aircraft, with one economy-only configuration and one with a small number of first class seats.

US carriers make up a large share of the global 737 MAX fleet.

Canada's flag carrier is preparing to launch its longest 737 MAX 8 flight, showing that airlines continue to use the jet to push the boundaries of narrowbody aviation. The route launches on December 13 and is between Vancouver International Airport (YVR) and Liberia International Airport (LIR) in Costa Rica. It covers 3,425 miles (5,512 km). The scheduled block time is seven hours and 20 minutes outbound, and eight hours and 55 minutes for the return journey. Air Canada hopes the new route will give it a strong position in the popular winter leisure travel market in Central America. The frequency will be between two and three times a week.

The route overtakes Montréal–Trudeau International Airport to Nantes Atlantique Airport (NTE). The transatlantic flight was Air Canada's previous longest 737 MAX 8 route. Other Air Canada 737 MAX 8 routes surpassing 3,000 miles (4,800 km) include trips to Shannon, Honolulu, Kahului, Brussels, Montego Bay, and Edinburgh.

The new route comes as the fleet transformation continues. “When customers step onto our aircraft, they should instantly feel a sense of comfort, care, and pride," said COO Mark Nasr. "This renewal program is about delivering that feeling consistently, across every flight. Every update is designed with our customers in mind, as we introduce an entirely new Air Canada Rouge product.”

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6164. American & Israir Partner On US-Israel Flights: Logical, But Limited

American Airlines and Israir Airlines have just announced plans to partner for flights between the United States and Israel. For now don’t expect huge implications, but over time, this has the potential to evolve.

American and Israir are launching a commercial partnership focused on enhanced travel options between Israel and the United States. The partnership is expected to expand in phases, delivering some benefits to customers. American plans to resume flights to Tel Aviv (TLV) as of late March 2027.

How is this partnership expected to play out?

For context, as of March 27, 2027, American plans to resume flights between New York and Tel Aviv, using the Boeing 777-200ER. Israir operates five weekly flights between Tel Aviv and New York, using an Airbus A330-200 (funny enough, the airline flies ex-American A330s, which the airline retired shortly after the start of the pandemic).

For those curious about the interiors of Israir’s A330s, below is a video of them (sorry, I don’t know what’s going on in the video, but I haven’t otherwise been able to find a cabin video).

Here’s how American’s SVP of Alliances, Anmol Bhargava, describes this:

“American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire. As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”

The dynamics of this partnership are interesting. There are a few things to keep in mind:

When it comes to the new partnership between American and Israir, here’s what’s I find noteworthy:

All-in-all, this is a pretty casual partnership. There’s no real downside here for American, since the carrier might just pick up a little bit of revenue on connecting Israir passengers beyond New York. Meanwhile Israir has a better framework for selling tickets beyond New York, which helps the carrier expand its potential customer base. But it is interesting how the codeshare is one-sided for now…

American Airlines and Israir Airlines are launching a partnership for flights between the United States and Israel. Israir will be codesharing on American’s flight between New York and Tel Aviv (when that resumes in late March 2027, in theory), while American will have an interline agreement with Israir, allowing Israir passengers to connect on American flights beyond New York.

We may see a closer level of cooperation between the two airlines in the future, including possible AAdvantage perks, but nothing has been finalized there yet. I wouldn’t read too much into this partnership for now, and think it falls more in the category of “better than nothing,” rather than anything beyond that.
