As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

BEST FOR GROCERIES AND U.S. STREAMING CASH BACK

Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express

As High As $300 Cash Back. Find Out Your Offer.

The Centurion Card from American Express has a reputation that few other cards can match. Its invitation-only application process, substantial fees and long list of perks have made the Amex “Black Card” a status symbol.

But you don't need a Centurion invitation to get better treatment at a hotel, airport lounge access or have someone help with a dinner reservation. Plenty of cards offer those benefits, often for a fraction of the cost.

Some Centurion perks remain difficult to replicate. Others are available with cards you might already have — and, in a few cases, another card can get you a higher level of status.

Here's what to know about the U.S. Centurion Card and the other ways to get its most useful benefits.

The information for the Centurion Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

There are personal and business versions of the Centurion Card. Both are invitation-only.

Amex doesn't publish a spending threshold that guarantees an invitation. Reports of the amounts required vary widely, and meeting a rumored minimum doesn't mean you'll be invited to apply.

If you're interested, you can contact Amex to ask about consideration. Just don't build your spending strategy around getting an invitation: There isn't a published qualification path you can follow as you would for airline or hotel elite status.

The has an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees). That's a substantial expense, but the Centurion Card costs considerably more.

The Centurion Card carries a $10,000 initiation fee and a $5,000 annual fee, bringing the first-year tab to $15,000 between the two.

At that price, the card needs to do considerably more than earn rewards. Whether it makes sense will depend on how much you use its services and benefits and how much you'd otherwise pay for them.

Related: Is the Amex Platinum worth its annual fee?

The Centurion Card has some impressive benefits, but its base earning rate of 1 Membership Rewards point per dollar spent isn't a reason to get it. The business version has additional earning opportunities, including a 1.5-point rate on eligible large purchases.

Other options for earning: You'll generally get better Membership Rewards point-earning potential in bonus categories with the or the .

For example, the Platinum earns 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through American Express Travel® (on up to $500,000 of those purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

And if you aren't loyal to Membership Rewards, the (see rates and fees) earns 4 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar spent on dining. The Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on all purchases.

Along with being a status marker itself, the Centurion Card offers complimentary elite status with several loyalty programs.

Marriott Bonvoy Gold elite status includes a 25% bonus on eligible base points, a welcome gift (at participating brands), space-available room upgrades and 2 p.m. late checkout (when available). It doesn't include complimentary breakfast or lounge access.

Other ways to get it: The and (with a $895 annual fee; see rates and fees) offer Gold status (enrollment required).

The , Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful® Credit Card and also provide automatic Gold status.

The provides the higher Platinum Elite tier automatically.

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Hilton Honors Diamond status includes a 100% bonus on eligible base points, executive lounge access (at properties with an eligible lounge) and space-available upgrades (that can include suites). Breakfast or food-and-beverage benefits vary by brand and region.

Although Diamond was once Hilton's highest elite tier, the program introduced Diamond Reserve in 2026. Still, Diamond remains valuable for frequent Hilton guests, particularly those staying at full-service properties.

Other ways to get it: You can get Diamond automatically by holding the , which has a $550 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Alternatively, you can earn it (through the end of the following calendar year) by spending $40,000 in a calendar year on the or the .

Centurion cardmembers can enroll for IHG One Rewards Diamond Elite status. Benefits include a 100% bonus on eligible base points, space-available upgrades and the option to choose breakfast for two as a welcome amenity (at participating brands). Diamond doesn't automatically include club lounge access.

Other ways to get it: You can earn Diamond Elite status by meeting these calendar-year spending requirements:

Platinum Medallion status offers eligible complimentary upgrades, priority airport services and 9 miles per dollar on eligible Delta-marketed flights.

Other ways to get it: There isn't a comparable automatic Platinum status benefit on a widely available U.S. credit card. However, you can fast-track your path with the , , or .

Each card provides 2,500 Medallion Qualification Dollars annually through MQD Headstart.

Both the Reserve and Business Reserve have a $650 annual fee (see rates and fees and rates and fees, respectively) and earn 1 MQD per $10 in eligible purchases, while the Platinum cards earn 1 MQD per $20.

Hertz Platinum offers benefits beyond the rental company's publicly earned tiers, including delivery services (at participating locations), and complimentary child seats and ski racks.

Other ways to get it: Hertz President’s Circle status is a more accessible alternative, although it isn't the same tier. It offers benefits such as vehicle upgrades (at participating locations) and a higher earning rate on eligible rentals.

You can enroll with the , , Venture X*, Capital One Venture X Business* and the Delta Reserve personal and business cards. U.S. consumer and business Platinum cardmembers who enrolled before July 9, 2026, must re-enroll through the Car Rental Privileges tile in their Amex benefits by Dec. 31, 2026. Allow up to 72 hours for processing.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Avis President's Club offers space-available double upgrades (on eligible reservations) and guaranteed availability of a car (up to full size with a confirmed reservation made at least 24 hours ahead).

Other ways to get it: The (see rates and fees) and United Club℠ Business Card provide access (after enrollment). United Premier Platinum, Premier 1K and Global Services members also qualify.

Most recently, the (see rates and fees) added complimentary Avis President's Club status for primary cardmembers (enrollment available through Aug. 31, 2028).

The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The Centurion Card offers up to $369 in Clear+ statement credits per calendar year. At standard prices of $219 for the main membership and $125 per additional adult, that fully covers a member and one other adult. Clear expedites identity verification at participating airport security checkpoints and event venues like stadiums.

Other ways to get it: The additional member coverage is unique to the Centurion Card. The , and also offer up to $219 in statement credits for Clear+ memberships (enrollment required; subject to auto-renewal).

Centurion cardmembers can enroll for a complimentary Equinox Destination Access membership, which includes an Equinox+ digital subscription.

Other ways to get it: The offers up to $300 in Equinox statement credits per calendar year for eligible U.S. club memberships or an Equinox+ subscription (enrollment required; subject to auto-renewal). It can cover part of your costs, but it doesn't replace a full club membership.

The Centurion Card offers an application fee credit of $120 for Global Entry or up to $85 for TSA PreCheck (every four or 4½ years, respectively).

Other ways to get it: A Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit is a fixture on many travel rewards cards, making this one of the easier Centurion benefits to replicate.

The personal Centurion Card offers up to $200 in annual Uber Cash for eligible U.S. rides and orders (issued as $15 monthly with an extra $20 in December). It also offers up to $120 in annual statement credits toward an eligible Uber One membership (subject to auto-renewal).

Other ways to get it: The personal provides the same benefits, while the offers $10 in monthly Uber Cash. (Uber Cash will be deposited into one Uber account when you add an eligible card as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card.)

Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings include daily breakfast for two, a $100 property credit toward eligible expenses, guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout and a room upgrade (when available).

Centurion enhancements at participating properties include an additional $200 credit (on stays of at least two consecutive nights; book by phone through Centurion services).

Other ways to get it: The and provide access to the standard FHR program.

There are also comparable hotel programs outside Amex. The and offer The Edit; the Venture X and Capital One Venture X Business offer the Premier Collection; and those with the (see rates and fees) and (see rates and fees) can book The Reserve by Citi Travel.

Eligible bookings can include breakfast for two, a $100 property credit and space-available room upgrades. Their rules differ — particularly around late checkout — so compare the benefits and total price before booking.

Related: A comparison of luxury hotel programs from credit card issuers

One of the Centurion Card's most appealing services is its concierge, which can help with requests such as restaurant reservations, event tickets and travel arrangements. How much that's worth depends on how often you use it and the assistance you receive.

Here’s what the original Points Guy himself, Brian Kelly, has to say about Ray, his Centurion concierge:

I’d guess that Ray saves me more than $20,000 a year. From knowing my preferred seat on a plane based on the layout of the cabin to advising hotels of my arrival and departure time, Ray is a jack of all trades. He’s arranged a tour in Beijing for me and my parents to visit the Forbidden City, Tiananmen Square and the Great Wall of China. He’s gotten me theater tickets, great concert seats (front row for Celine Dion) and hard-to-get restaurant reservations. Ray even takes on particularly cumbersome tasks, like locating my headphones when I lost them 10,000 miles from home.

Other ways to get it: While not quite as premium as the Centurion concierge, select Amex cardmembers can access an American Express Concierge for assistance purchasing event tickets, making reservations, booking travel and fulfilling shopping requests.

This perk is available on the , the and the .

Visa Infinite cards such as the and Venture X also provide concierge assistance.

Centurion† assistance at participating airports requires a first- or business-class ticket paid with the card through Amex Travel (and a request at least 74 hours ahead). Availability applies; expedited immigration isn't guaranteed.

Other ways to get it: You can purchase airport meet-and-greet services separately. That can be worth comparing if you need assistance on a particular trip, although you'll need to pay for the service yourself.

Centurion cardmembers receive access to Amex’s Global Lounge Collection, including Centurion Lounges, Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required), Escape Lounges, Plaza Premium lounges, Lufthansa lounges and Delta Sky Clubs.

Guest rules depend on the lounge. At U.S. Centurion Lounges and select international locations, Centurion cardmembers can bring their immediate family — a spouse or domestic partner and children under 18 — or up to two guests without charge. Delta Sky Club guests generally cost $50 each.

Centurion cardmembers also have access to reserved seating or dedicated spaces at select Centurion Lounges. Some locations go further: Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND) has a Centurion-only room with its own beverage station.

Other ways to get it: The and are the closest alternatives for access to the same lounge networks (enrollment may be required), with stricter visit and guest rules. Each provides 10 Delta Sky Club Visits per Medallion Year on eligible travel, compared with Centurion's unlimited eligible visits. Platinum cardmembers generally pay for Centurion Lounge guests unless they meet the $75,000 annual spending requirement for complimentary guest access.

The Delta Reserve personal and business cards offer 15 Sky Club Visits per Medallion Year and Centurion Lounge access on eligible Delta itineraries. Both those cards and the Amex Platinum cards can unlock unlimited Sky Club visits after $75,000 in eligible calendar-year purchases.

For lounge access outside Amex, the and offer Sapphire and Priority Pass lounge access, while the offers Priority Pass and four Admirals Club passes per calendar year. The Venture X and Venture X Business offer Capital One Lounges and Landings plus Priority Pass. None of these cards provides Centurion Lounge access.

The Centurion Card includes a PS membership and two complimentary Salon visits with a guest per calendar year (booked through Centurion services; after enrollment). The Salon is a shared lounge experience, distinct from a private suite.

PS operates at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and Miami International Airport (MIA).

Other ways to get it: You can book PS without a special credit card or a membership. Nonmember rates start at $1,295 per person for the Salon and $4,950 one-way for a private suite for up to four travelers (excluding taxes and fees).

Centurion cardmembers enjoy the highest level of travel and shopping protections American Express has to offer, including protection against trip delay and cancellation** and baggage delays*** as well as extended warranty*** and purchase protection.***

Other ways to get it: The and offer several overlapping protections; similar protections can be found on many cards across Amex’s portfolio.

**Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

**Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Centurion cardmembers receive access to dining opportunities and special events. However, several useful reservation benefits are available with less exclusive cards.

The Centurion Card combines some hard-to-replicate services with benefits you can get elsewhere.

If Hilton Diamond status is what matters to you, the is a straightforward alternative. If you want Marriott status, the actually provides a higher tier. And for lounge access and hotel booking perks, the and cover much of the same ground.

Ultimately, the Centurion Card's biggest differentiators are its exclusive experiences and personalized services. If those aren't priorities, you may be able to get the benefits you value most from a far less expensive card.

Start with the benefits you'll use, then work out which card provides them at a cost you can justify. You might not need an invitation to make your next trip more comfortable.

#6162. Amex Blue Cash Everyday Review: A No Annual Fee Card With Solid Bonus Categories

American Express is best known for its points-earning cards, but the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express proves that Amex can do cash back well too.

If you’re looking for a simple card that earns a solid return at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers, this one is worth a look. It has no annual fee (Rates & Fees), a decent welcome bonus, a great intro APR offer, and some useful bonus categories that cover a good chunk of everyday spending.

This post is my in-depth Blue Cash Everyday Card review, so I’ll cover the bonus categories, the credits and perks, and how this card compares to both the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express and the Citi Double Cash® Card.

Review: Learn more about the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express

First, here’s an overview of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday benefits and value proposition, from fees, to rewards, to the welcome bonus:

I also put together my list of pros and cons for the Blue Cash Everyday Card:

When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, eligibility rules, and fees, are major considerations. So below I’ll cover the details of that for the Amex Blue Cash Everyday.

The Amex Blue Cash Everyday is offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

That’s a reasonable bonus for a no annual fee card, and the spending requirement is low enough that most people should be able to hit it. However, it’s also not that much to get excited about, compared to some of the other welcome offers out there.

Amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. Here are the main rules to be aware of:

Amex also has a pre-application eligibility tool that lets you check whether you’ll be approved for the card without any impact on your credit score. This is worth using if you’re not sure that you’ll qualify.

The Blue Cash Everyday Card has no annual fee. Not the first year, not ever. That alone makes it worth considering as a long-term card in your wallet, even if it’s not your primary spender.

Holding no annual fee cards long term is also a great way to help your credit score. About 30% of your score comes from credit utilization (the more available credit you have but don’t use, the better), and 15% comes from credit history length (the older your average account age, the better). A no annual fee card you keep open for years helps on both fronts.

The Blue Cash Everyday Card does have foreign transaction fees (2.7%) (Rates & Fees), so I wouldn’t use it for purchases in foreign currencies. Stick to domestic spending with this one, and find a card with no foreign transaction fees if you’ll be spending time abroad.

The Amex Blue Cash Everyday has three main bonus categories, each earning 3% cash back on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%).

With the Blue Cash Everyday, you earn 3% back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). Earning 3% back at supermarkets with no annual fee is a solid deal, and this is one of the better no annual fee cards for U.S. supermarket spending.

As with most grocery bonus categories, this generally won’t include warehouse clubs (like Costco), superstores (like Walmart or Target), convenience stores, or discount stores. Traditional supermarkets and grocery chains are what you’re looking for.

With the Blue Cash Everyday, you also earn 3% back at U.S. gas stations on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This is one of the better no annual fee cards for gas station spending.

This is the bonus category that makes the Blue Cash Everyday stand out from its siblings. You earn 3% back on U.S. online retail purchases on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This covers purchases made on a website or app from a U.S. retail merchant that sells physical goods directly to consumers.

Given how much shopping happens online these days, this can be a really valuable category. You won’t find this bonus on many other cards.

For purchases outside the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is where the card falls short. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll definitely want to pair this with a card that offers a better return on everyday purchases.

With the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits at a rate of 1.0 cents per point, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem.

It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

Benefits and credits can certainly help with justifying holding onto credit cards. In the case of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you wouldn’t expect very valuable perks, given the card’s lack of an annual fee. However, it’s an area where I’d say the card actually exceeds expectations, and offers solid value.

The Blue Cash Everyday offers up to $7 back per month (up to $84 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled Blue Cash Everyday to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscriptions are subject to auto-renewal. If you already pay for any of those services, this is an easy credit to use. (Enrollment required)

You can also earn up to $15 per month (up to $180 per year) in statement credits when you purchase Home Chef meal solutions online with your Blue Cash Everyday Card. If you use Home Chef, this is a significant benefit. If you don’t, it’s probably not worth signing up just for the credit. (Enrollment required)

The Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 15 months from the date of account opening. After that, the variable APR is currently between 19.74% - 28.74% (Rates & Fees).

I generally recommend avoiding financing purchases through credit cards. But if a short-term 0% APR opportunity can help you manage a large purchase and you can pay it off before the rate increases, it’s a nice option to have.

Another card benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

Every Amex card gives you access to the Amex Offers program, which provides targeted deals with a variety of retailers. Different cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards means more chances to save.

I try to have as many Amex cards as possible specifically to take advantage of this. Having a no annual fee card like this is ideal, since the card isn’t costing you anything, but you’re still getting access to potentially valuable offers.

The Amex Blue Cash Everyday comes with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers purchase protection of up to $1,000 per covered purchase for up to 90 days from the purchase date. You need to pay with the card in order to take advantage of this coverage.

The Amex Blue Cash Everyday Card is a solid no annual fee cash back card with useful bonus categories at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers. The 3% rate in those categories is strong for a no annual fee card, and the Disney streaming credits, Home Chef credits, and Amex Offers add extra value on top.

While there are several reasons to consider the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there are also a couple of alternatives that I think are better for most people.

If you generally like the idea of the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there might still be a better play here. The Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express (learn more) is the premium version of the card, and it could be worth applying for it instead (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

The big question is whether the Preferred’s $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. annual fee (Rates & Fees) is worth the upgrade. If you spend at least $267 per month at U.S. supermarkets, the extra 3% (the Preferred earns 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases, then 1%) on groceries alone will cover the fee. The Preferred also adds 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming and 3% on transit, which the Everyday doesn’t offer.

On the flip side, the Everyday has two things the Preferred doesn’t: 3% on U.S. online retail purchases and a 0% intro APR offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and not as much grocery shopping, the Everyday could be the better card.

One nice thing is that you could start with the Blue Cash Preferred (with a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95.), and if the math doesn’t work out, downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after year one. That way you get the bigger welcome bonus and can test the higher earning rates.

While there are lots to like about the Blue Cash Everyday, it’s also not particularly well-rounded if you’re looking for an all-in-one cash back credit card.

The card offers 3% cash back at U.S. supermarkets, U.S. gas stations, and U.S. online retail purchases (up to certain limits), but on other purchases you’ll earn 1% cash back.

Everyone will have to crunch the numbers for themselves, but 1% cash back is pretty uncompetitive nowadays for savvy consumers. For example, the no annual fee Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

The Blue Cash Everyday wins in its bonus categories, earning 3% at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers compared to the Double Cash’s flat 2%. But the Double Cash wins everywhere else, earning 2% on all purchases versus just 1%.

If your spending is heavily concentrated in supermarkets, gas, and online shopping, the Blue Cash Everyday will earn you more. If your spending is more spread out across lots of different categories, the Double Cash’s flat 2% on everything will likely come out ahead.

The Double Cash also has a major advantage in flexibility. Its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners (in conjunction with a premium Citi card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card), giving those points the potential to be worth well more than 2 cents each. The Blue Cash Everyday’s rewards are purely cash back.

The ideal setup? Have both. Use the Blue Cash Everyday for supermarkets, gas, and online retail where it earns 3%, and the Double Cash for everything else at 2%.

I think the Blue Cash Everyday is a very decent cash back card with bonus categories most spenders can take advantage of. The card’s main weakness is the 1% rate on everything outside the bonus categories — and even on those categories once you reach the annual cap. For that reason, I’d recommend pairing it with a flat-rate card like the Citi Double Cash (2% on everything) to fill in the gaps. Together, they make a simple, effective, no annual fee credit card cash back setup.

If you find yourself spending more at supermarkets over time, you can always upgrade to the Blue Cash Preferred for that 6% supermarket rate. But for a no annual fee, low-maintenance starting point, the Blue Cash Everyday is a great choice.

#6161. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6158. Lufthansa Management Threatens To Massively Shrink Airline, Lay Off Employees

Lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization. 2026 was supposed to be an exciting turnaround year for Lufthansa, as it’s even the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

Unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great. Earlier this year, the carrier dealt with massive labor issues, and back-to-back-to-back strikes. Just a few months ago, the company’s senior management claimed it wanted to turn over a new leaf with labor relations, and stop fighting with employees, so that it could find long term solutions.

How is that working out? Well, Lufthansa pilots are just days from possibly being able to strike again, no agreement has been reached for long term peace with employees, and management is threatening to massively shrink its mainline operation. In other words, it’s just another day at Lufthansa!

Lufthansa and its pilots have been in negotiations for quite some time over the future of the company. As you’d expect, broadly speaking, negotiations revolve around pay and future flying opportunities. As you’d expect at any airline, employees want as much flying as possible, and as big of a fleet as possible, since that’s what maximizes their compensation.

The issue with Lufthansa Group management is that the company’s solution to everything is to simply create new, low cost subsidiaries. And if Lufthansa Group management doesn’t like the terms with its subsidiaries, then it just shuts down the subsidiaries and creates new ones.

So that brings us to the current issue. Essentially, Lufthansa’s problem is that the airline doesn’t make money on short haul flights, given high costs and intense competition. So we’ve seen the carrier increasingly outsourcing this flying to Lufthansa City Airlines, a subsidiary with lower operating costs, operating the same kinds of planes as you’ll see in the mainline fleet.

Lufthansa is asking its pilots to accept wage freezes, and is promising a certain level of career development opportunities. Pilots aren’t happy with what’s being proposed, so what’s Lufthansa’s solution?

Management is reportedly proposing a new plan to the supervisory board, which would see the core Lufthansa brand massively reduce its regional flying, and largely outsource this to lower cost operations, like Lufthansa City Airlines. The idea would be to make Lufthansa primarily a long haul airline, and then have much of the short haul flying be operated by a subsidiary.

Lufthansa’s mainline fleet currently consists of 260+ planes, with another 120+ planes on order. One proposal would see the mainline fleet reduced to 100 long haul aircraft and 100 short haul aircraft, with other planes being assigned to Lufthansa City Airlines.

One radical proposal could even see Lufthansa exclusively have a long haul fleet and ditch short haul flying, though it’s noted that this isn’t the most likely scenario, and it could take several years for something like that to be implemented.

Keep in mind that going back to 2017, Lufthansa had guaranteed pilots a minimum fleet size of 325 aircraft, but it terminated that agreement at the end of 2021. So it’s really hard for employees to trust any promises by management, when they can just be terminated.

There’s no denying that labor relations can be incredibly challenging, and that the economics of intra-Europe flying are also tough, when you have competitors like Ryanair, though Lufthansa doesn’t face nearly as much competition on that front as other carriers. Then again, Frankfurt (FRA) and Munich (MUC) aren’t exactly massively leisure destinations either.

Most airline employees want their company to succeed, and just want to be compensated fairly. Admittedly economics don’t always align. But what I find incredibly toxic is the approach taken by Lufthansa management. Let’s compare it to a marriage (which I think is a fair way to view the relationship between management and employees, since they’re “stuck” with one another).

Lufthansa’s approach is to constantly threaten employees by saying that “if you don’t do what we want, we’ll just get rid of you.” That’s simply not a good faith way to approach things. Why would Lufthansa employees trust management, when they’ve repeatedly torn up contracts, and shown employees they simply don’t care? It would be like threatening to leave your spouse every time you have an issue, rather than trying to find a solution.

Nothing against Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr personally, but I don’t understand how the board thinks he’s the best person for the job. Where’s the accountability for the endless management mistakes that have horribly impacted Lufthansa’s bottom line? Lufthansa’s employees are paying the price for the lack of success that comes as a result of all of Lufthansa’s errors, from the botched Allegris rollout, to Lufthansa’s very bad luck with new aircraft orders.

And before anyone says “oh, but the unions,” contrast what has happened at Lufthansa Group to what has happened at Air France-KLM, under the leadership of Ben Smith. Smith has now been CEO at Air France for over eight years, and there hasn’t been a single strike under his leadership. Under the previous Air France-KLM CEO, there were endless strikes, and the situation got so bad that senior executives were being chased up a fence and having their clothes ripped off.

This shows that good labor relations absolutely can happen, balancing the needs of employees and the company. But it requires showing employees that you actually care about the company and their future. What was one of Smith’s first orders of business when he took the job at Air France-KLM? He eliminated Joon, the low cost carrier at the airline that was supposed to basically be a labor arbitrage opportunity. That was a way to show employees how much he respected them, and that he wanted a fair agreement, rather than one that would undermine them.

Meanwhile Spohr’s solution to literally everything is to just threaten to start new subsidiaries or shut down existing subsidiaries. The irony is that Spohr started his career as a pilot, so you’d think he’d have respect for employees, having been on the other side. But clearly once he became senior management, his love for aviation turned into disdain for employees.

A few months ago, Lufthansa management claimed it wanted to turn over a new leaf when it comes to labor relations. That didn’t last long, because now the airline is back to its “do what we say or we’ll create a new subsidiary” approach.

I don’t have a strong opinion on the exact negotiations as such. Obviously it’s a tough time for aviation, and intra-Europe flying is challenging. But if you ask me, the toxicity that has been created by Lufthansa management due to the lack of good faith negotiations just can’t be undone.

If your only solution to everything is “oh, we’ll create a new subsidiary,” and if that doesn’t work, maybe it’s time for a new strategy. The fact that American CEO Robert Isom and Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr still have their jobs are two of the industry’s greatest mysteries.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s latest threat to employees?

#6157. Considering The Bilt Palladium Card? Here’s Why You Should Apply Soon…

The Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) is the most premium card in the Bilt credit card portfolio, and personally, it’s one of my all-around favorite cards (Rates & Fees). If you’ve been on the fence about picking up this very lucrative card, I’d highly recommend applying ASAP, and definitely before the end of 2026. Let me explain…

The Bilt Palladium Card is one of my favorite credit cards, and it’s the card that gets the most of my spending. Just to cover some of the very basics, the card has a $495 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following value proposition at the moment:

For me, the logic of picking up this card is pretty straightforward, and I’ve shared that in much more detail. The idea is that the combination of the 2x points plus 4% back in the form of Bilt Cash is an unrivaled return on spending, especially given the value of Bilt points. Spending on Bilt cards also earns you Bilt elite status, and that unlocks better Rent Day promotions.

On the most basic level, that Bilt Cash earns me 1x points per dollar spent on my housing payments (without any sort of fee), plus I take advantage of the Points Accelerator feature, which earns me an extra 1x points per dollar spent up to five times per year, by redeeming $200 in Bilt Cash. In other words, this card earns me 3x points on up to $25,000 of spending per year, plus I’m being rewarded on my housing spending.

Points with Bilt rack up really quickly, so if you spend quite a bit on credit cards, I do think this is tough to beat. And this doesn’t even account for the value of the hotel credit, as you can stack the credit card’s hotel credit with some Bilt Cash to get an even bigger discount on a hotel stay.

As I’ve covered, changes are coming to Bilt as of 2027. While the changes are being made in the name of “simplifying” things, I’d argue that it only creates even more complexity, at least for existing members. Essentially, starting in 2027, Bilt members will earn points for their housing payment as a percentage of their card spending, in lieu of earning 4% back in Bilt Cash on all their spending.

The good news is that through December 31, 2026, you can still opt into the old system for being rewarded, and that will then be honored in 2027 and beyond. This applies both to existing cardmembers, and those who pick up the card before then, and select this as their earnings preference.

The idea is that if you opt into this grandfathered system and have the Bilt Palladium Card:

Just as an example, I have more Bilt Cash than I can redeem (at least as someone who is scared of helicopters, and who finds Blacklane to be overpriced even with the Bilt Cash redemption options). However, the Bilt Cash I earn gets me 1x points on all my housing payments, maxed out Points Accelerator redemptions, elevated Rent Day offers, and Lyft and Walgreens redemptions, so I get $120 in credit with each business per year.

I think the Bilt Palladium can still absolutely be worth it under the new system, where you’d be rewarded on housing payments per the below, and would also earn $600 in Bilt Cash annually (starting in 2027), but without the 4% back in the form of Bilt Cash on spending.

So if the Bilt Palladium Card has at all been on your radar, this would definitely be the time to apply. After all, this is what will allow you to maximize value on the card in the long run.

Bilt is making some program changes as of 2027, which are a mixed bag. From my perspective, the biggest loss is that cardmembers are by default being switched from a system where they earn points plus flexible Bilt Cash for their spending, to one where they earn points plus rewards at a certain rate toward housing payments.

At least for me, the old system is definitely better, and the good news is that through the end of 2026, you can continue to opt into the old system of earning points plus Bilt Cash for spending, and then that will be honored in 2027 and beyond. This applies not just to those who already have the card, but also those who open the card before the end of the year. So if the Bilt Palladium Card has been on your radar, I’d recommend applying in the near future.

The next frontier for the Airbus A321XLR is South America.

After opening dozens of new transatlantic routes, the long-range narrow-body will make its debut with LATAM Airlines in March 2027. The airline has yet to say which routes the XLRs will fly, but executives have previously outlined opportunities to connect the U.S. and South America.

The suites include 19-inch personal entertainment screens, Bluetooth connectivity and in-seat charging options.

Economy features 13-inch screens at each of the 126 seats, which are supplied by Recaro, plus Bluetooth connectivity and USB-C outlets. The cabin includes 36 extra-legroom seats.

“The Airbus A321XLR allows us to take our value proposition to the next level and elevate the travel experience for our passengers,” said Paulo Miranda, the chief customer officer of LATAM, in a statement. He described the interior, which features red, orange and blue hues, as “inspired by South America.”

LATAM executives have said it could fly the XLR on routes into the U.S. from its hub at Jorge Chavez International Airport (LIM) in Lima. However, those plans were called into question in May over the addition of a "connection fee" at LIM.

The airline and Delta serve six U.S. destinations from LIM: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Orlando International Airport (MCO) and, since January 2026, Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

LATAM did not comment on specific route plans for the XLR.

The XLR is the second new airplane type for LATAM in as many years. The airline took delivery of its first Embraer E195-E2 in October. It will use the small jet to expand its feeder network in Brazil and support additional long-haul, intercontinental flying.

#6155. Highest-Paying Airline Jobs: 5 Roles That Earn Six Figures Without Flying

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

The aviation industry depends on far more than pilots and cabin crew to keep its aircraft flying and its global operations running smoothly. Behind every departure is a network of highly skilled professionals responsible for flight planning, aircraft maintenance, complex electronic systems, engineering, and the financial decisions that keep airlines competitive. Many of these essential roles take place well away from the passenger cabin, yet they offer rewarding career opportunities and considerable earning potential.

From FAA-certificated aircraft dispatchers and experienced maintenance technicians to avionics specialists, aerospace engineers, and airline revenue analysts, these professionals bring specialized knowledge to one of the world's most demanding industries. Here are five aviation careers that offer attractive salaries without requiring individuals to become pilots.

Airlines must do more than fill seats to remain profitable. Behind the ticket prices passengers see when booking a flight is a team of revenue management and pricing analysts, whose job is to determine how much an airline should charge for each seat and when. These professionals study passenger demand, booking trends, competitor fares, and historical sales data to help airlines maximize revenue across their networks.

According to JetBlue Airways, its revenue management team is responsible for maximizing ticket revenue on every flight, with analysts working across two main areas: pricing and yield management. Pricing analysts monitor competitor fares and adjust the airline's own pricing strategies, while yield analysts manage seat availability and fare levels to make the most of passenger demand. American Airlines similarly describes the role as using data-driven pricing and inventory strategies to improve revenue performance across assigned markets.

The work is highly analytical and generally requires a degree in finance, economics, business, mathematics, or a related field, alongside strong data analysis skills. JetBlue lists a salary range of $58,000 to $86,000 (£44,200 to £65,700) for its Associate Analyst Revenue Management position, while ZipRecruiter lists airline revenue management analyst salaries across a range of current vacancies.

A 172-foot tailless prototype chased efficiency as early pilots wrestled with yaw instability and control limits.

An aircraft dispatcher is an FAA-certificated airline operations professional. These individuals are closely involved in the planning, releasing, monitoring, and continual support of flights during ground, in-air, and arrival operations. GlassDoor states that these aviation professionals earn between $73,000 (£55.500) and $137,000 (£104,200K) per year.

Adding to this, Thrust Flight School says that their salary primarily depends on the airline they work for and how many years of service they have under their belt. They state that first-year pay at most regional carriers is between $41,000 (£31,200) and $52,000 (£39,600) a year. However, major US airlines will pay a first-year airline dispatcher approximately $95,000 (£72,300), with the top of the pay scale reaching around $170,000 (£129,300) for an 11-year veteran.

According to the US Aviation Academy, "the dispatcher and pilot in command share defined responsibility for preflight planning, delay, and dispatch release." Additionally, a dispatcher "monitors each assigned flight, provides information needed for safety, and participates in cancellation or redispatch decisions when a flight cannot safely operate or continue as planned."

Reviews relevant weather, NOTAMs, operational issues, aircraft information, and flights assigned to the desk.

Evaluates route, fuel, weather, alternates, aircraft information, and other dispatch requirements.

Tracks several assigned flights and watches for information or conditions that may affect their safe operation.

Exchanges operational information with flight crews and coordinates with other airline operational resources as required.

Evaluates weather, airport, routing, aircraft, or other changes and helps determine the applicable operational response.

Transfers relevant information about active flights and operational concerns when responsibilities move to another qualified dispatcher.

Generally, dispatchers perform their work in centralized airline operations environments rather than airport control towers. Airlines use different terms for the areas in which they work, including Operations Control Centers (OCCs), System Operations Control Centers (SOCCs), and Network Operations Centers.

To grasp the scale of the daily operations managed by dispatchers, American Airlines, generally considered the largest airline in the United States, notes that it maintains a staff of 600 dispatchers and operations specialists. American states that it operates "6,000 daily flights to more than 350 destinations in more than 60 countries," with its dispatchers playing an integral role in supporting these global operations.

United Airlines has been rebuilding its presence at its former Cleveland Hopkins hub.

Flight safety involves numerous overlapping and interconnected layers of responsibility, expertise, security, and regulation. A crucial component of the aviation ecosystem is the generally unseen aircraft mechanic. USAFacts explains that the oft-stated expression "flying is safer than driving" is absolutely valid. The site states that in "2023, 33 plane passengers were injured over 773 billion miles of air travel. Put another way, you could circle the globe over 940,000 times for every one airplane injury."

This level of consistent safety depends a great deal on the skill, proficiency, and training of aircraft mechanics, as well as their continual learning and honing of their skills. These professionals ensure that every aircraft, from nose to tail and fuselage top to wheel, is rigorously inspected, repaired, and cleared for flight.

For their essential services and expertise, US Aviation Academy reports that the median annual salary for an aircraft mechanic was $79,870 in May 2025. Further, they add that the mean annual wage was $84,740 (£64,742), while the median hourly wage was $38.40 (£29.34). The bottom 10% of this skill pool earned less than $48,780 (£37,263), while the highest 10% earned more than $128,890 (£98,498).

While the pay for this line of work is rewarding, North America is facing a growing shortage of aviation maintenance personnel. The Aviation Technician Education Council reports that there is a widening deficit of certificated aircraft mechanics, which is expected to increase from approximately 9,100 this year to 20,000 by 2030, representing 12% of anticipated demand. Fortunately, the Council reports that the FAA issued 11,103 new mechanic certificates in 2025, 23.2% more than in 2024 and the highest annual total since the agency began publishing the data.

It'll mark the carrier's return to this city after nine months. Find out more now!

On a daily basis, major airlines entrust their $306 million to $442 million (£234 million to £338 million) Boeing 777s (or similar aircraft) to the capable hands of their avionics technicians. These men and women install navigation, radio, radar, and autopilot systems. They also repair or replace faulty wiring, sensors, and instrument panels, and carry out post-repair testing.

One miswired transponder or uncalibrated altimeter can render an aircraft unfit to fly or affect crucial systems while airborne. Modern passenger jets are equipped with hundreds of interconnected electronic components, and a failure in one can potentially affect others. Like maintenance technicians, their counterparts in avionics require a great deal of training, usually 18 to 24 months. Their courses cover circuit analysis, digital electronics, and the proper use of diagnostic equipment.

Upon completion, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) states that these skilled workers earn a median annual wage of $82,280 (£62,862), based on 2025 statistics. Further, the BLS reports that there were approximately 19,800 avionics technicians employed in the US in 2025, and the future outlook for this profession is encouraging.

To this point, the Bureau notes that employment among avionics technicians is projected to grow by 9% between 2025 and 2035. It also projects about "13,100 openings for aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians. . .projected each year, on average, over the decade. Many of those openings are expected to result from the need to replace workers who transfer to different occupations or exit the labor force, such as to retire."

The Qatari donated 747-8 and two aging 747-200 aircraft were all seen in Manila before the recent trilateral summit.

When we watch an aircraft fly overhead, land at an airport, or enter the cabin, everything we look at and touch has been meticulously designed with ergonomics, functionality, mechanical integrity, and comfort in mind. Those behind this specialized planning are aeronautics engineers.

These men and women earn a median annual salary of $134,960 (£103,126), according to the BLS. Employment in this field is projected to grow by 8% between 2025 and 2035, with approximately 3,800 openings across the industry each year over the decade. Many of these openings are likely to result from the need to replace engineers who transfer to different occupations or retire.

The Museum of Flight states that there are five types of engineers within the field of aviation who contribute to the design, manufacture, and support of aircraft. These include industrial, structural, avionics, acoustics, and sales engineers. Each brings a different area of expertise to the industry, from improving manufacturing processes and ensuring structural integrity to developing complex electronic systems and reducing aircraft noise. Together, these specialists help ensure that modern aircraft are not only capable of flying safely but are also efficient, functional, and commercially viable.

Industrial engineers plan and improve how aircraft are manufactured, ensuring they are produced as efficiently and safely as possible. Structural engineers design the frame of an aircraft, making sure it is structurally sound enough to withstand the rigors of not only flight but also harsh landings and taxiing. Avionics engineers map out the electrical systems that span the aircraft, from the cockpit to the tail. Finally, acoustics engineers use testing to identify ways to reduce noise inside and outside an aircraft. Sales engineers, meanwhile, work directly with customers, explaining aircraft capabilities and helping airlines, governments, and other buyers select aircraft that meet their operational requirements.

#6154. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#6153. Influencer Uses AI To Score American First Class Upgrade… And Overpays

There’s no denying that AI holds a lot of potential to transform how we go about our every day life, both for better or worse.

People are increasingly using AI for travel planning, but here’s an interesting twist on that. Can AI help you find award flights and secure upgrades? It’s something I’d like to study in a bit more detail and write about in the coming weeks, but I just saw a post on Instagram that piqued my interest, so I figured it would make for a fun story. Consider this just a little teaser, for the time being.

An Instagram user with 1.5 million followers who promises to help people master AI has just published a video about how “ChatGPT upgraded me to first class.” Now, that’s not as exciting as it sounds on the surface. The idea is simply that ChatGPT helped someone secure an upgrade through the standard means — it’s not like ChatGPT used his/her/their charm to sweet talk someone into an upgrade by dressing up nicely. 😉

Let me actually just quote the description of the video, which covers most of the content:

What happens when you ask ChatGPT to upgrade your flight to first class?

I tried this on my flight in two weeks and it actually worked.

Go to ChatGPT and switch from Chat to Work at the top. Start a new chat and give it your airline and confirmation code.

Prompt 1:“Ask me every question you need about my credit cards, my miles, and my memberships, and map out every upgrade currency I own for this exact flight.”

ChatGPT shows you that you’ve been sitting on upgrade power this whole time without even knowing it.

Prompt 2:“Now look up my exact flight, check how empty the first class cabin is, and tell me every way I can get up there, ranked from free to cheapest.”

Prompt 3:“Now go get me the upgrade. Use my miles if the math is worth it, and place the upgrade bid at the smartest number, or get me on the upgrade list right now.”

ChatGPT opens its own browser, logs into your airline, and actually chases that seat for you while you sit back and do nothing.

You can watch the video for yourself below.

A post shared by Maverick Maltin | AI & ChatGPT (@mavgpt)

I don’t want to suggest AI isn’t useful, but I’d say that the example given is actually very poor. First of all, let’s be clear about what’s actually going on here. He had booked a business class ticket on American from Los Angeles (LAX) to London (LHR), and then upgraded to first class.

Now, in the first place, something isn’t fully accurate here:

Okay, maybe he edited the dates, or something, which is fine, and it’s besides the point, but as a detail oriented airline nerd, I couldn’t help but notice those things. Anyway, let’s assume this is all accurate:

To me, this is kind of where AI falls flat, and it isn’t the correct way to use it. The prompt was reportedly to “use my miles if the math is worth it, and place the upgrade bid at the smartest number, or get me on the upgrade list right now.” This is where I get confused — you’d think that AI would be able to scour reviews online, and see that American first class isn’t (well, or wasn’t) really viewed as a product that’s worth the premium.

If AI were really providing useful advice here, it would’ve recommend waitlisting with the systemwide upgrade, and otherwise recommending the guy save his 70,000 miles, and use them for something else. While there are definitely some strong use cases for AI, I think this is actually a pretty poor showing of what it can do.

By the way, keep in mind that under United’s updated contract of carriage, using AI to help service reservations is banned, and could potentially get your ticket canceled. Whether there’s any enforcement of that remains to be seen.

While the thought of using AI to score an upgrade might sound great, don’t count on it actually getting you the best deal. An AI whiz claims he has the secret to using AI to upgrade to first class. All AI did was use the instant upgrade offer that was available directly on American’s website, and it didn’t even encourage him to skip the upgrade due to it not being worthwhile, or waitlisting the upgrade with a systemwide upgrade, which is objectively a much better deal than 70,000 miles.

What do you make of this AI “assistance” for a first class upgrade?

No matter how you feel about deportations as such, having them go down in this way for someone who simply overstayed their visa is a step too far, in my opinion. I mean, it’s one thing if we’re talking about a violent criminal on some sort of watch list, but that’s clearly not the case here.

Our four-year-old is currently at the age where he asks “why” in response to everything… and he has a lot of good questions that often make me step back and think “oh, that’s a good point.” I put myself in the situation of being on the jet bridge here as a parent, and trying to explain what was going on.

And here’s the thing — it’s one thing if these people were in uniform and identifying themselves, but when you have people who refuse to identify themselves, it’s an especially bad look. It reminds me of another incident we recently saw at Las Vegas Airport (LAS). Like, is this person being robbed in the terminal, or is this an official law enforcement operation?

A post shared by Chris Motley (@motleymodel)

On Saturday, an Alaska Airlines flight was delayed by a few hours after ICE agents stormed a jet bridge to arrest someone, leading to a larger fight, which also caused more arrests. It’s one thing if such a disruptive operation were targeting a violent criminal, but is this really the way that someone who overstays a visa should be apprehended?

The Port of Seattle has expressed outrage over how this was handled, while ICE is outraged at how its “brave law enforcement” is facing increasing violence from the public.
